metadata.title: IR band map for CO₂ hydrogenation
metadata.description: Approximate band positions for surface and gas-phase species in CO₂ hydrogenation. Exact positions depend on support, coverage, and reaction conditions. The asterisk (*) denotes a surface-bound species.

co2_hydrogenation_rwgs_ch4.label: CO₂ to CO/CH₄
co2_hydrogenation_rwgs_ch4.note: Everything the RWGS and CO₂ methanation story touches.

fluids.label: Gases + Fluids
fluids.note: The free molecules only: reactants and products as gas or fluid, no surface species. Their adsorbed bands are left out too.

co_methanation.label: CO methanation
co_methanation.note: Everything the CO₂ methanation story touches.

carbonate.label: Carbonate
carbonate.note: Monodentate and bidentate coordination are `topology` on the band, not separate species.

formic_acid.label: Formic acid
formic_acid.note: Formate that has kept its proton: HCOOH adsorbed without dissociating. The C=O stretch near 1700 to 1730 cm⁻¹ is what separates it from formate, which has no localised carbonyl at all, so an absorption in that window is the test for whether the acid dissociated on contact.

methylenebisoxy.label: Methylenebisoxy
methylenebisoxy.note: Formate one hydrogenation step further on, with both oxygens still held by the surface; also written dioxymethylene. It sits between HCOO* and H₂CO* on the methanol path, and because it cannot be dosed, the sources that name it rest on a calculated frequency plus a band that rises and falls out of step with the formate it comes from.

acyl.label: Acyl
acyl.note: Generic acyl group; the R is left open because the sources do not fix it.

hydroxyl.label: Surface OH
hydroxyl.note: A hydroxyl on an oxide surface. Deliberately not split into isolated and hydrogen-bonded: that split needs evidence a source actually gives, and where a paper does resolve several hydroxyls it resolves them by the cation they sit on, which the claim records as its site.

o_vacancy.label: Oxygen vacancy
o_vacancy.note: A missing lattice oxygen in a reducible oxide, and the electrons left behind with it. Not a molecule and it has no normal modes; it is here because the electron trapped in it absorbs infrared light, which puts a band on the chart that belongs to no adsorbate.

silica.label: Silica framework
silica.note: The Si-O-Si network of a silica or silicate support itself, not anything adsorbed on it. Here for the same reason as the oxygen vacancy: its overtones put bands on the chart that no adsorbate made.

hydride.label: Hydride
hydride.note: Metal hydride from heterolytic H₂ dissociation. Written metal-generic; the band names the element.

cu_0.label: Cu⁰
cu_0.note: Metallic copper. Carries ν(CO) roughly 40–80 cm⁻¹ below the Cu⁺ carbonyl.

ga.label: Ga
ga.note: A Ga centre carrying a hydride, written as Ga-H with no charge in the sources that report it. Neither Ga⁰ nor Ga³⁺ is asserted, which is why this entry has no kind and no oxidation state; use ga_3p only where the paper states the cation. The two coordinations below are the resolved forms of it: a claim that says only Ga is a claim that did not separate them.

ga_tet.label: Ga(t)
ga_tet.note: Tetrahedrally coordinated gallium, the Ga(t) of β-Ga₂O₃. Its hydride and hydroxyl sit about 25 and 150 cm⁻¹ above those of the octahedral site, which is how the two are told apart.

ga_oct.label: Ga(o)
ga_oct.note: Octahedrally coordinated gallium, the Ga(o) of β-Ga₂O₃. Coordinatively unsaturated at the surface, which is why it, and not the saturated tetrahedral site, is where H₂ dissociates in the calculations.

cu_1p.label: Cu⁺
cu_1p.note: The carbonyl marker that separates a partly oxidised copper surface from Cu⁰.

cu_2p.label: Cu²⁺
cu_2p.note: Fully oxidised copper, carrying a carbonyl some 25 cm⁻¹ above the Cu⁺ one. Rare in this dataset, because a working methanol catalyst is reduced: where a source reports it on one, it is claiming a minority site that survived the reduction, and the claim is worth reading against the Cu⁺ assignment it sits next to.

h_bronsted.label: H⁺ (Brønsted)
h_bronsted.note: A proton-donating surface hydroxyl, as opposed to the Lewis-acidic cations above.

o_vac.label: Vₒ
o_vac.note: A bare oxygen vacancy. Listed on its own so ensembles can point at it.

o_vac_1p.label: Vₒ⁺
o_vac_1p.note: An oxygen vacancy that has given up one of its two electrons, the donor centre whose photoionization to the conduction band is the broad electronic absorption under an operando Cu/ZnO spectrum. Its concentration, not just its existence, is what the band measures.

zn_ovac_hf.label: Zn–Vₒ–Hf
zn_ovac_hf.note: An oxygen vacancy flanked by Zn and Hf: the two cations and the vacancy act as one site.

pt0_ceo2_interface.label: Pt⁰-CeO₂ interface
pt0_ceo2_interface.note: The perimeter where the metal particle meets the reducible support, not either phase alone.

zno_1mx.label: ZnO₁₋ₓ
zno_1mx.note: Zinc oxide after reduction, carrying the oxygen vacancies that stoichiometric ZnO does not. Recorded apart from zno because the distinction is the point wherever it is named: the defects are what the strong metal-support interaction with copper creates, and what the infrared background reports on.

hfo2.label: HfO₂
hfo2.note: Hafnia, ZrO₂'s chemical twin. Monoclinic when precipitated and calcined on its own; the Zn-doped solid solutions are cubic and are the znhfox sample, not this.

ga2o3.label: Ga₂O₃
ga2o3.note: Gallia, as a constituent of a promoted catalyst and as a sample in its own right. The β polymorph carries both gallium coordinations, which is why hydride and hydroxyl bands on it come in pairs.

fe3o4.label: Fe₃O₄
fe3o4.note: Magnetite with no termination stated. The two facet variants below point at it, and all three are the same compound: only the cut differs.

fe3o4_001.label: Fe₃O₄(001)
fe3o4_001.note: Magnetite cut on the (001) plane. The formula is the whole chemistry: (001) is a termination, not a composition, so this entry and fe3o4_111 are the same compound differently cut. It is a phase for that reason, named by formula like any other bare oxide; `parts` points at plain fe3o4 so a query for magnetite reaches it.

fe3o4_111.label: Fe₃O₄(111)
fe3o4_111.note: The other termination measured in the same study, chemically identical to fe3o4_001. They are separate entries because the two cuts expose different Fe spacings and carry different formate geometries, which is a structural difference and not a compositional one.

cu_sio2.label: Cu/SiO₂
cu_sio2.note: Copper on silica with no promoter. Silica is close to inert here, so this is the reference against which a promoter's effect is read, and it is listed with Cu⁰ alone: the sources that pair it with a promoted counterpart find no Cu⁺ carbonyl on it at all.

cuga_sio2.label: Cu-Ga₂O₃/SiO₂
cuga_sio2.note: Ga₂O₃-promoted Cu on silica, published as a loading series written CuGa(x) where x is the Ga/(Cu+Ga) molar ratio. The family is recorded here and the member named in the note, because the distinction the spectra turn on is against the Ga-free cu_sio2 rather than between members: the Cu⁺ carbonyl is absent without Ga and its area grows with the loading.

cu_gazrox.label: Cu-GaZrOₓ
cu_gazrox.note: Coprecipitated Cu-Ga-Zr mixed oxide, around 20 wt% Cu. Sources publish it as a series with different Ga and Zr loadings, written Cu-GaZrOₓ-Z where Z is Zr/(Zr+Cu+Ga) as a molar percentage; the family is recorded here and the individual member named in the note, since the distinction the spectra turn on is against the Cu-free GaZrOₓ rather than between members.

znhfox.label: ZnHfOₓ
znhfox.note: Co-precipitated Zn–Hf mixed oxide, published as a series written xZnHfOₓ with x the Zn/(Zn+Hf) molar percentage. Up to about 35 mol% it is Zn-doped cubic HfO₂ in solid solution; above 40 mol% bulk ZnO segregates and carries HfOₓ clusters on its surface. One key for the family, with the member named in the note, because the IR bands of both regimes agree within a few wavenumbers and that agreement is the claim the spectra turn on. ZnO is not listed as a part: the low-Zn members contain none.

gazrox.label: GaZrOₓ
gazrox.note: The Cu-free counterpart of the Cu-GaZrOₓ series, 48 wt% Ga and 25 wt% Zr. Run to separate what the oxide does from what Cu does.

la_al2o3.label: La-Al₂O₃
la_al2o3.note: Lanthanum-doped alumina; the doping stabilises the support rather than adding an IR-visible site.

ru_na2o_al2o3.label: Ru/"Na₂O"/Al₂O₃
ru_na2o_al2o3.note: The sodium-promoted counterpart of Ru/Al₂O₃; the quotes are the authors' own.

co_siralox.label: Co/Siralox
co_siralox.note: Cobalt on Siralox, a commercial silica-alumina of 5% SiO₂ and 95% Al₂O₃. Kept apart from co_al2o3: the support differs, and so does the carbonyl position reported on it. SiO₂ is not listed as a part: at 5% it is a dopant of the alumina, not a phase of its own.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ asymmetric stretch (νₐₛ) — R-branch envelope maximum at ~2360 cm⁻¹, paired with the P-branch at ~2335. The Q-branch between them is symmetry-forbidden — see co2_asym_q. Saturates at high pCO₂.

references.note: νₐₛ band origin (00011←00001) at 2349 cm⁻¹ (Table 2); 2360 here is the R-branch envelope maximum, not a single measured line.
Gas-phase CO₂ R-branch observed at 2373 cm⁻¹ during DRM at 600°C (Table 3); reactant concentration marker.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ asymmetric stretch (νₐₛ) — Q-branch at the 2349 cm⁻¹ band origin. Forbidden by symmetry for this Σᵤ⁺←Σg⁺ parallel transition, so no rotational line actually appears here; marks the gap between the R- and P-branch envelopes.

references.note: νₐₛ band origin (00011←00001) at 2349 cm⁻¹ (Table 2) — the forbidden Q-branch position itself, not an observed line.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ asymmetric stretch (νₐₛ) — P-branch envelope maximum at ~2335 cm⁻¹, paired with the R-branch at ~2360. Same forbidden-Q gap as the R-branch entry — see co2_asym_q. Saturates at high pCO₂.

references.note: νₐₛ band origin (00011←00001) at 2349 cm⁻¹ (Table 2); 2335 here is the P-branch envelope maximum, not a single measured line.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ bending fundamental (δ) — R-branch (ΔJ = +1) at ~700 cm⁻¹. Higher-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the P-branch at ~660. Q-branch is allowed (Σ→Π transition) and appears as a sharp spike at ~667 between P and R envelopes.

references.note: Reports the δ band origin (01101←00001) at 667 cm⁻¹ (Table 2); ~700 here is the R-branch envelope maximum.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ bending fundamental (δ) — Q-branch (ΔJ = 0) at ~667 cm⁻¹. Sharp, intense spike between P and R envelopes; allowed because this mode is a Σ→Π (perpendicular) transition. Saturates very quickly at modest pCO₂.

references.note: Q-branch coincides with the reported δ band origin (01101←00001) at 667 cm⁻¹ (Table 2) — the fundamental bending mode.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ bending fundamental (δ) — P-branch (ΔJ = −1) at ~660 cm⁻¹. Lower-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~700. Atmospheric CO₂ in the beam path contributes to this region; routinely seen even with good purging.

references.note: Reports the δ band origin (01101←00001) at 667 cm⁻¹ (Table 2); ~660 here is the P-branch envelope maximum.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3730 cm⁻¹; (νₛ + νₐₛ) R-branch — upper Fermi-resonance component, R-side. Useful for high-pressure quantification when the νₐₛ fundamental saturates. Genuinely Fermi-coupled to the 2δ+νₐₛ doublet below (~3600 cm⁻¹), not just two coincidentally nearby combination bands — see co2_sym for why the resonance between νₛ and 2δ carries through into both bands' own +νₐₛ combination levels.

references.note: Table 2 gives the band origin of the ν₁+ν₃ combination at ~3715 cm⁻¹. For a Σ to Σ transition that origin is the gap between the two branches rather than a position in either, and the paper tabulates no maximum for the R branch, so no wavenumber is taken from it here. DRIFTS of pure KBr under 10 bar CO₂ at 278 K.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3699 cm⁻¹; (νₛ + νₐₛ) P-branch — upper Fermi-resonance component, P-side. P/R-branch separation ~30 cm⁻¹; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~3730. See co2_sym for why this combination doublet is genuinely Fermi-coupled to the 2δ+νₐₛ one below, not just nearby.

references.note: Table 2 gives the band origin of the ν₁+ν₃ combination at ~3715 cm⁻¹. For a Σ to Σ transition that origin is the gap between the two branches rather than a position in either, and the paper tabulates no maximum for the P branch, so no wavenumber is taken from it here. DRIFTS of pure KBr under 10 bar CO₂ at 278 K.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3627 cm⁻¹; (2δ + νₐₛ) R-branch — lower Fermi-resonance component, R-side. Separation between Fermi pair (3730 vs 3627) ~107 cm⁻¹ is fixed. See co2_bend_overtone for why this combination doublet is genuinely Fermi-coupled to the νₛ+νₐₛ one above, not just nearby.

references.note: Table 2 gives the band origin of the 2ν₂+ν₃ combination at ~3613 cm⁻¹. For a Σ to Σ transition that origin is the gap between the two branches rather than a position in either, and the paper tabulates no maximum for the R branch, so no wavenumber is taken from it here. DRIFTS of pure KBr under 10 bar CO₂ at 278 K.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3597 cm⁻¹; (2δ + νₐₛ) P-branch — lower Fermi-resonance component, P-side. P/R-branch separation ~30 cm⁻¹; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~3627. See co2_bend_overtone for why this combination doublet is genuinely Fermi-coupled to the νₛ+νₐₛ one above, not just nearby.

references.note: Table 2 gives the band origin of the 2ν₂+ν₃ combination at ~3613 cm⁻¹. For a Σ to Σ transition that origin is the gap between the two branches rather than a position in either, and the paper tabulates no maximum for the P branch, so no wavenumber is taken from it here. DRIFTS of pure KBr under 10 bar CO₂ at 278 K.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination of the infrared-forbidden symmetric stretch with the bend: the combined level is dipole-allowed although the stretch alone is not. Very strong and narrow, the most prominent gas band between 2200 and 1900 cm⁻¹, sitting squarely in the linear metal-carbonyl window, and the most misassigned band in this atlas: eight published studies read this one position as adsorbed CO. Its intensity tracks CO₂ pressure rather than anything on the surface, which is the discriminator. Heat and pressurise the cell and the same molecule adds hot and difference bands, absent at ambient conditions, at 2130 and 2094 cm⁻¹ among the carbonyls and 1079, 1050, 973 and 948 cm⁻¹ among the methoxy bands.

references.note: Table 3, band J: very strong and narrow, the Q branch of the 11101←00001 transition of ¹²C¹⁶O₂ and the most intense combination band in the range, which every other intensity in the paper is normalised to. Table 1 lists three earlier papers and Table 4 five more that assigned this position to adsorbed CO. Weaker gas bands are left undrawn: 2112 cm⁻¹, either this transition’s R branch or the P branch of a hot band, which the source cannot separate; 2130 and 2094 cm⁻¹, hot bands published as CO on Cu⁺ and on Cu(110); and 1933 and 1920 cm⁻¹, the 11102←00001 pair published as CO on a CuZn alloy. All of them need CO₂ pressure to show at all.

Table S5 and Fig. S17 (operando DRIFTS, Cu/SiO₂ and CuGa(0.20), 220 to 280 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): listed as gas-phase CO₂ and cited to Fehr et al., the source of the claim on this band above. Worth recording as a second reading of the same position: it sits between the two gas CO branches at 2177 and 2112 cm⁻¹ in the same spectra, exactly where a CO band on a copper catalyst would be looked for, and this paper does not read it as one.

bands.description: The P branch of the same combination band whose Q branch sits 20 cm⁻¹ above. Equally intense but broad rather than narrow, so it reads as a shoulder or a hump rather than the peak its partner makes, and it is the less often reported of the two for that reason. It has still been published four times as adsorbed CO, once specifically as CO at a copper-zinc interface. Rotational structure resolves it at 0.5 cm⁻¹; at the 4 cm⁻¹ usual in catalysis it is one smooth band.

references.note: Table 3 of a DRIFTS spectrum of pure KBr under 10 bar of CO₂ at 278 K, 4 cm⁻¹ and 64 scans, intensities normalised to the 2077 cm⁻¹ band. Very strong and broad, the P branch of the 11101←00001 transition whose Q branch is the 2077 cm⁻¹ normalisation band. Table 4 lists four papers that assigned this position to adsorbed CO, against eight for the Q branch.

bands.description: A difference band: the asymmetric stretch reached from a molecule already holding two quanta of bend rather than from the ground state. Only a fraction of a percent of molecules sit in that level at room temperature, but the transition is strong enough that a pressurised cell still shows it clearly, and it climbs steeply with both pressure and temperature. It lands on the methoxy C-O stretch and on gas-phase methanol, which is the worst place for a CO₂ artefact in a methanol experiment: it rises with temperature, which is what a methanol signal is expected to do.

based_on.label: less two quanta of the bend: a difference band, from an already vibrating molecule

references.note: Table 3 of a DRIFTS spectrum of pure KBr under 10 bar of CO₂ at 278 K, 4 cm⁻¹ and 64 scans, intensities normalised to the 2077 cm⁻¹ band. Bands P and Q: R branch at about 1079 cm⁻¹ and Q branch at about 1050 cm⁻¹, both strong and broad, transition 00011←10002 of ¹²C¹⁶O₂, both marked as rising strongly with temperature. Drawn as one band because at the resolution of a catalysis experiment the pair is one feature. Table 4 lists the first as having been published as methoxy on ZnO and the second as gaseous methanol or a methoxy species.

bands.description: The companion difference band, reached from a molecule already holding one quantum of the symmetric stretch: an R and a P branch straddling 960 cm⁻¹, strong and broad in a pressurised cell. Both have been published as methoxy bound to copper. The test is the temperature: these climb steeply as the cell is heated, because heating populates the level they start from, and a surface methoxy population does not behave that way.

based_on.label: less one quantum of the symmetric stretch: a difference band, from an already vibrating molecule

references.note: Table 3 of a DRIFTS spectrum of pure KBr under 10 bar of CO₂ at 278 K, 4 cm⁻¹ and 64 scans, intensities normalised to the 2077 cm⁻¹ band. Bands R and S: R branch at about 973 cm⁻¹ and P branch at about 948 cm⁻¹, both strong and broad, transition 00011←10001 of ¹²C¹⁶O₂, both marked as rising strongly with temperature. Table 4 lists them as having been published as methoxy on Cu and on Cu⁰.

bands.description: Symmetric stretch of CO₂ held linearly on a surface cation through one oxygen, without becoming carbonate. In the free molecule this mode is infrared-forbidden and seen only in Raman; binding breaks the symmetry just enough to give it a weak infrared band. The asymmetric stretch near 2340 cm⁻¹ is far stronger and the usual marker of adsorbed CO₂, but it sits under the gas-phase band. This one falls among the carbonate and formate symmetric stretches, where it is easily read as one of them.

references.note: Fig. S56f and the accompanying SI text (ZnO reference, 20 vol% CO₂ in N₂, 320 °C, 20 bar): assigned to linearly adsorbed CO₂, CO₂*, citing earlier work. The paper names the species and not the mode; the symmetric stretch is the only CO₂ fundamental near this position. It lies between the bidentate and polydentate carbonate bands of the same spectrum.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ symmetric stretch, strictly IR-forbidden (Σg⁺, no dipole change) and seen only in Raman. It is carried here as the explicit parent of the νₛ+νₐₛ combination band and as the Fermi partner of the bending overtone: the cubic anharmonic term that mixes those two also mixes their +νₐₛ combination levels, which is why the pair of combination doublets higher up is marked as a Fermi pair as well.

references.note: Table 3 and Fig. 3: formally infrared-inactive, yet observed in DRIFTS of pure KBr once the CO₂ pressure passes roughly 10 bar, together with its Fermi partner at 1285 cm⁻¹ and with an intensity ratio near 1.0 at 30 bar. The pair is the Fermi resonance itself made visible: the deperturbed ν₁ lies at 1337 cm⁻¹ and is pushed up to 1388, while 2ν₂ falls from 1334 to 1285 cm⁻¹. Both grow with pressure and, unlike every combination band in the same spectrum, weaken as the temperature rises.

Text and Fig. 2: the upper Fermi dyad band at ca. 1387 cm⁻¹, neat CO₂ flowed through a Si/glass microreactor chip, 785 nm excitation, 5–14 MPa at 298, 307 and 323 K, so across the gas, liquid and supercritical states. The position depends on pressure and temperature: read off Fig. 2, it runs from about 1389 cm⁻¹ (5 MPa, 323 K) down to about 1386 cm⁻¹ in the dense fluid, stepping abruptly at the gas–liquid (298 K, 6–7 MPa) and gas–supercritical (307 K, 7–8 MPa) transitions and falling smoothly at 323 K. The paper calls the pair the Fermi dyad without saying which component is ν₁; the split follows the atlas. With 5 % each of cyclohexene and H₂ (10 MPa, 305–318 K) the dyad sits at or below the liquid value at 305 K, which the paper reads as phase segregation.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ bending overtone, the l=0 component of two bending quanta. Like νₛ it is IR-forbidden and seen only in Raman. It is in genuine Fermi resonance with νₛ: the cubic anharmonic coupling pushes both away from their uncoupled positions to the observed 1285/1388 cm⁻¹ split, and the same coupling carries up into the two combination doublets near 3700 and 3600 cm⁻¹.

references.note: Table 3 and Fig. 3: the lower Fermi component, formally infrared-inactive but seen in DRIFTS above roughly 10 bar of CO₂ alongside the 1388 cm⁻¹ partner. Its unperturbed position is 1334 cm⁻¹, and the resonance pushes it down to 1285. Both bands weaken with rising temperature, which is what separates them from the combination bands nearby.

Text and Fig. 2: the lower Fermi dyad band at ca. 1284 cm⁻¹, the same on-chip measurement as its partner at 1387 cm⁻¹ (neat CO₂ in a Si/glass microreactor, 785 nm excitation, 5–14 MPa at 298, 307 and 323 K, through gas, liquid and supercritical CO₂). The position depends on pressure and temperature: read off Fig. 2, it runs from about 1285 cm⁻¹ (5 MPa, 323 K) down to about 1281.5 cm⁻¹ in the dense liquid, with the same abrupt steps at the phase transitions as the upper band and a smooth trend at 323 K. The paper does not say which component is 2ν₂; the split follows the atlas.

bands.description: Gas-phase CO stretch (ν) — R-branch (ΔJ = +1) at ~2170 cm⁻¹. Higher-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the P-branch at ~2115. Q-branch forbidden for diatomic CO (Σ→Σ transition), leaving a characteristic gap at ~2143 cm⁻¹ between R and P branches — see co_stretch_q.

references.note: Fig. 5a and Section 3.3 (Spectra-Tech DRIFTS cell, 14% Co/Al₂O₃ at 220 °C, 30% CO + 60% H₂ + 10% Ar, ambient pressure). The paper uses this branch to measure the cell: over a mirror at 80 °C it is 2.97 times weaker than in a 10 cm transmission gas cell, which puts the beam's path through gas above the bed at 3.37 cm of a 3.50 cm total, leaving about 1.3 mm through the bed voids (Fig. 4). Fig. 6 shows the envelope widening as its height falls between 50 and 400 °C over SiC. The gas temperature cannot be fitted to one value, because the beam crosses gas from the 80 °C windows to the hot bed.

Table S5 and Fig. S17 (operando DRIFTS, Cu/SiO₂ and CuGa(0.20), 220 to 280 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): the R branch of the CO the reaction is making, paired with the P branch at 2112 cm⁻¹. Both grow with temperature in the same proportion on the promoted and unpromoted catalysts, which matches the kinetics: Ga raises the methanol rate by about an order of magnitude and leaves the CO rate alone.

bands.description: Gas-phase CO stretch (ν) — Q-branch at the ~2143 cm⁻¹ band origin. Forbidden by symmetry for this Σ→Σ transition, so no rotational line actually appears here; marks the gap between the R- and P-branch envelopes.

Gas-phase CO stretch (ν) — P-branch (ΔJ = −1) at ~2115 cm⁻¹. Lower-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~2170. P/R splitting ~55 cm⁻¹ at room temperature; envelope broadens and shifts intensity to higher-J lines as temperature increases (Maxwell–Boltzmann redistribution). Same forbidden-Q gap as the R-branch entry — see co_stretch_q.

references.note: Fig. 5a and Section 3.3 (14% Co/Al₂O₃ at 220 °C, 30% CO + 60% H₂ + 10% Ar, ambient pressure): the P branch, on the high side of linear CO on cobalt. Subtracting a CO(g) spectrum taken over SiC at 50 °C fails at every scaling tried (Fig. 5b to 5e): too little leaves the branches positive, too much makes them negative and still leaves a spurious positive band near 2220 cm⁻¹, because the rotational envelope changes shape with temperature. A SiC reference at 220 °C in the same feed subtracts cleanly (Fig. 7b); the feed matters too, since H₂ conducts heat differently from CO and Ar.

Table S5 and Fig. S17 (operando DRIFTS, Cu/SiO₂ and CuGa(0.20), 220 to 280 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): the P branch of product CO, with its R branch at 2177 cm⁻¹, a 65 cm⁻¹ separation. On this catalyst it overlaps the window where linear Cu⁰-CO is reported at high coverage, 2120 cm⁻¹ in the same paper's CO-dosing experiments, so the gas envelope has to be accounted for before any adsorbed carbonyl is read out of a spectrum taken under reaction.

bands.description: Gas methane asymmetric C-H stretch (νₐₛ, ν₃, T₂ mode): the sharp Q branch at the ~3019 cm⁻¹ band origin, the feature gas methane is usually recognised by. Active in both IR and Raman. Its rotational P and R branches spread either side (ch4g_asym_p, ch4g_asym_r), and the P side overlaps νₛ near 2917 cm⁻¹ in Raman.

references.note: Table 3: νₛ(–CH₃) at 3016 cm⁻¹; gas-phase CH₄ C-H stretch during DRM at 600°C over Ni-Ce-Fe/La-Al₂O₃.

Table No. 71, methane, Td: selected value 3019 cm⁻¹, uncertainty code A (0 to 1 cm⁻¹), the triply degenerate f₂ stretch. This is the one methane fundamental measured cleanly in both: infrared 3018.9 cm⁻¹ and Raman 3019.5 cm⁻¹. It is the band a catalysis spectrum actually sees, since ν₁ and ν₂ have no infrared intensity of their own.

Sect. 4.2 and Fig. 3: the anisotropic part of the pentad Raman spectrum is dominated by the fundamental ν₃ (F₂), whose rotational structure depends strongly on temperature (room temperature to 700 K in Fig. 3); spontaneous Raman of ¹²CH₄ in a heated gas cell at low density (about one amagat, below 1 atm to avoid line mixing), 4 W argon-ion laser, room temperature to 900 K. The fit needed only the zeroth-order ν₃ polarisability operator. The text gives no position for the band.

bands.description: Gas methane asymmetric C-H stretch (ν₃, T₂): the P branch, the rotational lines below the 3019 cm⁻¹ Q branch (ch4g_asym). Active in IR and Raman. It overlaps νₛ near 2917 cm⁻¹ and the δₛ+δₐₛ combination near 2830 cm⁻¹, so a band here is not by itself νₛ. In Raman the wings also hold the O and S branches (ΔJ = −2, +2), which a spherical top allows alongside P and R; the atlas files the low side under P and the high side under R.

references.note: Sect. 4.2, Fig. 3 and Fig. 13 (totally depolarised, room temperature): ν₃ dominates the anisotropic pentad spectrum, and its low-wavenumber rotational wing is this side of the sharp Q branch. The paper names neither the branches nor their positions, so no number is recorded; the wing gains lines as the temperature rises (Fig. 3, up to 700 K). Spontaneous Raman, gas cell at about one amagat, 4 W argon-ion laser.

bands.description: Gas methane asymmetric C-H stretch (ν₃, T₂): the R branch, the rotational lines above the 3019 cm⁻¹ Q branch (ch4g_asym). Active in IR and Raman. In Raman the wings also hold the O and S branches (ΔJ = −2, +2), which a spherical top allows alongside P and R; the atlas files the low side under P and the high side under R.

references.note: Sect. 4.2, Fig. 3 and Fig. 13 (totally depolarised, room temperature): the high-wavenumber rotational wing of ν₃, the stronger of the two sides in Fig. 13. The paper names neither the branches nor their positions, so no number is recorded. Spontaneous Raman, gas cell at about one amagat, 4 W argon-ion laser, room temperature to 900 K.

bands.description: Gas methane asymmetric bending (δₐₛ, T₂ mode) at ~1306 cm⁻¹.

references.note: Table 3: ν(CH₄, Gaseous) at 1306 cm⁻¹; present across all catalysts under DRM at 600°C; gas-phase CH₄ concentration marker.

Table No. 71, methane, Td: selected value 1306 cm⁻¹ for the f₂ deformation, infrared 1306.2 cm⁻¹ and no Raman entry. Its uncertainty code is C, 3 to 6 cm⁻¹, against A for the other three fundamentals — the least precisely fixed of methane’s four, which is worth knowing before reading a few wavenumbers of shift as chemistry.

bands.description: Gas methane symmetric bending (δₛ, E mode) at ~1534 cm⁻¹. IR-forbidden by symmetry: E in Td has no T₂ component, so the mode carries no dipole derivative of its own. It is still seen in the infrared, near 1533 cm⁻¹, by borrowing intensity through Coriolis coupling to the δₐₛ bend below it — a reminder that a forbidden mode is one with no dipole derivative, not one that is never observed. In Raman it is the band that dominates the dyad. This entry is the Q branch; in Raman its P and R wings (ch4g_bend_sym_p, ch4g_bend_sym_r) spread either side.

references.note: Table No. 71, methane, Td: selected value 1534 cm⁻¹, uncertainty code A (0 to 1 cm⁻¹). The infrared column reads "ia, 1533" with a footnote saying the band is observed in the infrared through Coriolis interaction with ν₄, and the Raman column gives 1533.6 cm⁻¹. So the compilation records both that the mode is formally inactive and that it is nonetheless seen: the two are not in conflict.

Sect. 4.1 and Fig. 2: the Raman spectrum of the dyad (about 1300–1850 cm⁻¹) is totally anisotropic and dominated by ν₂ (E), a strong central Q branch with rotational lines on both sides; spontaneous Raman of ¹²CH₄ in a heated gas cell at low density (about one amagat, below 1 atm to avoid line mixing), 4 W argon-ion laser, room temperature to 900 K. No number is recorded: the text’s only one, “near 1530 cm⁻¹”, is printed against ν₄, which the same paragraph calls very weak in Raman and leaves out of the fit. That it belongs to ν₂ is the atlas’s reading, not the paper’s.

bands.description: Gas methane symmetric bend (δₛ, ν₂, E): the P branch, the rotational lines below the ~1533 cm⁻¹ Q branch (ch4g_bend_sym). Raman-active and IR-forbidden like the Q branch. Its low end runs towards δₐₛ near 1306 cm⁻¹, which is very weak in Raman. In Raman the wings also hold the O and S branches (ΔJ = −2, +2), which a spherical top allows alongside P and R; the atlas files the low side under P and the high side under R.

references.note: Sect. 4.1, Fig. 2 and Fig. 13: the dyad Raman spectrum is totally anisotropic and dominated by ν₂, with rotational lines on both sides of its strong Q branch; this is the low-wavenumber side. The paper names neither the branches nor their positions, so no number is recorded. Spontaneous Raman, gas cell at about one amagat, 4 W argon-ion laser.

bands.description: Gas methane symmetric bend (δₛ, ν₂, E): the R branch, the rotational lines above the ~1533 cm⁻¹ Q branch (ch4g_bend_sym). Raman-active and IR-forbidden like the Q branch. In Raman the wings also hold the O and S branches (ΔJ = −2, +2), which a spherical top allows alongside P and R; the atlas files the low side under P and the high side under R.

references.note: Sect. 4.1, Fig. 2 and Fig. 13: the high-wavenumber side of the ν₂ dyad spectrum, where Fig. 2 shows the longer, better separated series of rotational lines. The paper names neither the branches nor their positions, so no number is recorded. Spontaneous Raman, gas cell at about one amagat, 4 W argon-ion laser.

bands.description: Gas methane symmetric C-H stretch (νₛ, A₁ mode) at ~2917 cm⁻¹. IR-forbidden by symmetry (A₁ in Td has no T₂/dipole component); observed only in Raman spectroscopy.

references.note: Table No. 71, methane, Td: selected value 2917 cm⁻¹ with uncertainty code A, the compilation's best grade at 0 to 1 cm⁻¹. The infrared column is marked ia, inactive, and the number comes from the Raman column at 2917.0 cm⁻¹, so this is a Raman position rather than an infrared one, and the technique is recorded as raman. The compilation itself selects rather than measures.

Recommended experimental value 0.362 eV (≈2920 cm⁻¹) for ν₁, A₁ symmetric stretch, Raman-active/IR-inactive; calculated value 0.390 eV (≈3146 cm⁻¹) given alongside it in the same table. Two caveats. The paper is a close-coupling calculation of electron-impact vibrational excitation and reports no infrared spectrum of its own: the mode energies are inputs it adopts from the literature, so it is a secondary source for this position. And no copy is on file and the article is paywalled, so this row could not be checked against the paper on the pass that added the compilation value above.

Sect. 4.2, Fig. 3 and conclusions: the strong isotropic ν₁ (A₁) band near 2916 cm⁻¹, a Q branch that is unresolved at the 0.3 cm⁻¹ apparatus width; spontaneous Raman of ¹²CH₄ in a heated gas cell at low density (about one amagat, below 1 atm to avoid line mixing), 4 W argon-ion laser, room temperature to 900 K. The stimulated Raman spectrum at 0.08 bar and 300 K (Fig. 8) resolves that Q branch into lines between about 2916.5 and 2918 cm⁻¹, read off the figure. From 400 K on, hot bands ν₁+nνᵢ−nνᵢ fill 2900–2920 cm⁻¹ (ν₁+ν₄−ν₄ at 2913 cm⁻¹, Fig. 10), which is what makes the band a thermometer. ν₁ is in Fermi resonance with 2ν₂ and 2ν₄ and in Dennison resonance with ν₂+ν₄.

bands.description: Gas methane combination band ν₃+ν₄ (δₐₛ+νₐₛ) near 4300 cm⁻¹, the strongest band of the octad in the near-infrared and in Raman. F₂×F₂ gives A₁, E and F₂ components, so it is active in both. Close neighbours in the same polyad blur it: ν₁+ν₄ on the low side, ν₁+ν₂ on the high side, and ν₂+ν₃ further up near 4540 cm⁻¹, which is where δₛ+νₐₛ belongs, not here. Useful for quantification when νₐₛ saturates; often outside a standard DRIFTS window. This entry is the Q branch, the sharp centre; its P and R wings are ch4g_combo_p and ch4g_combo_r.

references.note: Sect. 4.3, Figs. 11–13 and Table 5: the octad Raman spectrum (Table 1: about 3500–4700 cm⁻¹), extremely weak, recorded over 1 h with the 300 gr/mm grating at room temperature, in the same gas cell (about one amagat, 4 W argon-ion laser). Its fit needed six first-order polarisability operators: ν₁+ν₂ (E), ν₁+ν₄ (F₂), ν₂+ν₃ (F₂) and the A₁, E and F₂ components of ν₃+ν₄, the E one the largest. The paper ties no peak to a band, so reading the main feature near 4300 cm⁻¹ as ν₃+ν₄ is the atlas’s inference, and no number is recorded. Its neighbours ν₁+ν₄ and ν₁+ν₂ fill the wings.

bands.description: Gas methane combination band ν₃+ν₄ (δₐₛ+νₐₛ): the P branch, the rotational lines below the ~4310 cm⁻¹ Q branch (ch4g_combo). Active in IR and Raman. It overlaps ν₁+ν₄ of the same polyad, so a feature here is not necessarily ν₃+ν₄. In Raman the wings also hold O and S branches (ΔJ = −2, +2); the atlas files the low side under P and the high side under R.

references.note: Sect. 4.3 and Figs. 11–13: the low-wavenumber side of the octad feature near 4300 cm⁻¹, at room temperature in the same gas cell (about one amagat, 4 W argon-ion laser, 300 gr/mm grating). The paper names neither the branches nor their positions and ties no peak to a band, so reading this wing as ν₃+ν₄ is the atlas’s inference, and no number is recorded.

bands.description: Gas methane combination band ν₃+ν₄ (δₐₛ+νₐₛ): the R branch, the rotational lines above the ~4310 cm⁻¹ Q branch (ch4g_combo). Active in IR and Raman. It overlaps ν₁+ν₂ of the same polyad, so a feature here is not necessarily ν₃+ν₄. In Raman the wings also hold O and S branches (ΔJ = −2, +2); the atlas files the low side under P and the high side under R.

references.note: Sect. 4.3 and Figs. 11–13: the high-wavenumber side of the octad feature near 4300 cm⁻¹, at room temperature in the same gas cell (about one amagat, 4 W argon-ion laser, 300 gr/mm grating). The paper names neither the branches nor their positions and ties no peak to a band, so reading this wing as ν₃+ν₄ is the atlas’s inference, and no number is recorded.

bands.description: CO bonded end-on to a single metal atom, the commonest coordination and usually the strongest, sharpest band in a CO-probe spectrum. Its position follows metal to CO π-backdonation: more backdonation into the 2π* orbital weakens the C-O bond and pushes the band down, while electron-poor or oxidised sites push it up, so metal identity, oxidation state, coordination and coverage all move it. ¹³CO substitution shifts it by tens of cm⁻¹, the standard check that a band really is a CO stretch.

references.note: Fig. 3a (KRS-5 transmission cell, −160 °C, 0.15 mbar CO, static vacuum, after in-situ reduction in H₂ at 300 °C and evacuation to 10⁻⁴ mbar): three components resolved by deconvolution and assigned together to linear Cu⁰-CO. The 2065 and 2030 cm⁻¹ pair, read as very unsaturated centres, loses intensity as Ga is loaded, which the authors attribute to Ga₂O₃ diffusing to the edge of the Cu particle. Low coverage and static vacuum put these about 20 cm⁻¹ below the 2120 cm⁻¹ the same group measures for this site under flowing CO; they note the Cu⁰ to Cu⁺ separation stays near 27 cm⁻¹ either way.

Figs. S3a and S3b (DRIFTS, 5% CO/He flowing at 20 mL min⁻¹, 1 bar, 15 min): linear Cu⁰-CO at high coverage under dynamic conditions, at 30 °C on every catalyst and at 220 °C only on CuGa(0.15) and CuGa(0.20). That it survives to 220 °C on the Ga-rich samples alone is the paper's evidence that the promoter strengthens CO binding; on the unpromoted Cu and on loadings up to Ga/(Cu+Ga) = 0.10 no adsorbed CO is left at that temperature. Desorption at both temperatures is followed in Figs. S5 and S6.

Fig. 5a and Section 3.3 (14% Co/Al₂O₃ reduced in situ at 450 °C for 1 h in 60% H₂/Ar, then 220 °C, 30% CO + 60% H₂ + 10% Ar at ambient pressure, steady state, background SiC under Ar at the same temperature): a large band of linear, on-top CO on metallic cobalt, with ill-resolved bridged and multibonded CO below it. The CO(g) branches sit on its high side and only subtract cleanly against SiC at the same temperature and feed (Fig. 7b), which then leaves the same flat baseline as removing CO altogether (Fig. 7c).

Fig. 4c and Section 3.2 (14% Co/Siralox reduced at 450 °C, then 80 °C, 30% CO + 60% H₂ + 10% Ar, background the same sample under Ar): the paper describes a cobalt carbonyl signal spanning 2100 to 1700 cm⁻¹ and gives only its maximum, without separating linear from bridged CO. It is recorded here because the maximum is where linear CO sits. The spectrum was taken to measure the gas path through the bed, for which the CO(g) R branch was used because it does not overlap this signal.

Linear ¹²CO on Pt at the Pt–CeO₂ interface at 2053 cm⁻¹ (Fig. 4a); red-shifted by ~20–30 cm⁻¹ from bare Pt (2070–2080 cm⁻¹) due to enhanced π-backdonation from highly reduced CeO₂. SSITKA confirms this species is an active intermediate in RWGS: isotopic exchange rate matches CO(g) production rate. The ¹³C-substituted counterpart is filed separately — see ν(¹³CO) linear (μ₁).

On-top (linear, μ₁) CO on Pd nanoparticles typically observed at 2080–2090 cm⁻¹ (Introduction, citing prior SFG work), distinct from this same paper's own focus on bridge-site coverage dependence (see co_bridge_mu2).

Fig. 7a, and Figs. S18/S19 in the SI (MCR-resolved, He+CO₂ vs H₂+He switching, 230 °C, 20 bar): CO* on metallic Cu at 2113 cm⁻¹ (Cu–Zn/SiO₂), 2115 cm⁻¹ (Cu/SiO₂) and 2108 cm⁻¹ (Cu–In/SiO₂), produced in situ by decomposition of κ²-HCOO*(Cu) rather than dosed — its rise mirrors the formate component's decay, making it the spectroscopic signature of the unselective RWGS branch. Invisible at steady state on every catalyst (it is hydrogenated away as fast as it forms); only the alternating CO₂/H₂ transient exposes it. Notably absent from Fig. S20 (Cu–Ga/SiO₂): no CO* is detectable on the Ga-promoted catalyst at all, which the authors take as the direct cause of its 94% methanol selectivity — formate spillover to Ga³⁺ outruns formate decomposition on Cu, so the RWGS branch never opens.

bands.description: Atop CO carrying ¹³C, the same stretch as the ¹²CO band roughly 45 to 50 cm⁻¹ lower. It exists mainly as the landing zone for the standard isotope check: substitute ¹³CO and see whether a candidate band moves by the predicted amount. It matters in its own right in ¹³CO₂ transient work, where the shifted position is where the surface CO pool is tracked.

references.note: Linear ¹³CO on Pt at the Pt–CeO₂ interface at 2005 cm⁻¹ under ¹³CO₂, against 2053 cm⁻¹ for the ¹²CO form on the same sites — a 48 cm⁻¹ shift, matching the expected value for a linear CO stretch and confirming the assignment.

bands.description: Bridging CO coordinated between two metal atoms. Lower frequency than linear CO due to increased metal→CO π-backdonation from the extra metal center, and typically broader/weaker than the linear band, often appearing as a shoulder below it rather than a fully separate peak. Usually emerges or grows in only at higher CO coverage, since it needs two adjacent free metal sites to form.

references.note: Fig. 5a and Section 3.3 (14% Co/Al₂O₃ at 220 °C, 30% CO + 60% H₂ + 10% Ar, ambient pressure, steady state): ill-resolved bands below 2000 cm⁻¹ that the paper associates with bridged and multibonded CO, citing its own earlier work, without giving a position or separating the two. Not resolved from the tail of the linear band.

DFT-calculated (scaled) frequency of bridge-bound CO at the edges of Pd nanoparticles, growing from ~1886 cm⁻¹ for an isolated bridge CO up to ~1989 cm⁻¹ once the edge bridge sites are fully occupied by coadsorbed CO (Table 1) — matching the experimentally observed 1980–1990 cm⁻¹ band and implying particles ≥3 nm to host the necessary 10–12-CO edge ensemble.

Fig. 3a (KRS-5 transmission cell, −160 °C, 0.15 mbar CO, static vacuum): bridge-bound (Cu⁰)₂-CO, the fourth and weakest component of the deconvolution, some 140 cm⁻¹ below the linear band on the same surface. It needs the low temperature to be seen at all; nothing at this position survives into the flowing-CO experiments at 30 and 220 °C.

bands.description: Three-fold hollow CO coordinated to three metal atoms at once. Stronger multi-center π-backdonation shifts ν(CO) well below both bridge and linear adsorption. Generally needs a close-packed facet to offer this coordination geometry at all, and tends to appear or strengthen with increasing coverage as simpler one- and two-fold sites fill up first.

references.note: DFT-calculated (scaled) frequencies of 3-fold hollow CO on Pd(111)-type facets/nanoparticles range from ~1802–1815 cm⁻¹ at low coverage up to ~1902 cm⁻¹ at the high-coverage (2×2)-3CO structure (0.75 ML), tracking the same coverage-dependent blue shift seen for bridge-bound CO.

bands.description: Four-fold hollow CO coordinated to four metal atoms at once — a comparatively rare coordination geometry, since it needs a specific square arrangement of surface atoms to form. Exhibits the lowest ν(CO) frequencies among metal-CO adsorption modes, since backdonation from four neighbors at once weakens the C-O bond more than any other coordination geometry.

Linear CO adsorbed on a Lewis-acidic cation site rather than a reduced metal atom. Markedly less metal→CO π-backdonation than on a metallic surface, blue-shifting ν(CO) above the free-gas value (2143 cm⁻¹) rather than below it — the opposite direction from every metallic-surface CO band in this dataset. Position correlates with the cation's formal charge and Lewis acidity, making this band a widely used spectroscopic probe of acid-site strength and oxidation state; the same ¹³CO isotope-shift check used for metallic sites applies here too.

references.note: Fig. 3a (KRS-5 transmission cell, −160 °C, 0.15 mbar CO, static vacuum): a Cu⁺-CO feature absent from the unpromoted Cu/SiO₂ and appearing only once Ga is loaded. Its deconvoluted area gives the Cu⁺/(Cu⁰+Cu⁺) ratio, which rises linearly with Ga content (Fig. S4a) and correlates with TOF(MeOH) at every temperature with R² above 0.95 (Fig. 3b). Assigned to Cu⁺ at the Cu-Ga₂O₃ interface, the proposed methanol active site.

Figs. S3a and S3b (DRIFTS, 5% CO/He flowing at 20 mL min⁻¹, 1 bar): the same Cu⁺ carbonyl at high coverage under flowing CO, 22 cm⁻¹ above the value the transmission experiment gives at −160 °C under vacuum. The paper attributes the whole difference to coverage and to static against dynamic conditions rather than to a different site, noting that the Cu⁰ to Cu⁺ separation holds near 27 cm⁻¹ in both. Well defined at 220 °C only on CuGa(0.15) and CuGa(0.20); desorption is followed in Figs. S5 and S6.

Figs. S3c, S4b and S10 (DRIFTS, 10% CO₂/Ar at 20 mL min⁻¹, 3 bar, 220 °C): no CO is fed here. The band grows when CO₂ alone is dosed, and the authors read it as Cu⁺(O)-CO, the carbonyl left on a Cu⁺ that has just split CO₂ into CO* and O*. It is absent on the unpromoted catalyst and its area scales with Ga loading (Fig. S4b), which is their evidence that the interfacial Cu⁺ dissociates CO₂ without hydrogen. Switching to H₂/Ar moves it to 2165 cm⁻¹ (Fig. S10), read as the oxygen being taken off the site.

Table S5 and Fig. S10 (operando DRIFTS, 220 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): Cu⁺-CO under working conditions, and the band the 2196 cm⁻¹ Cu⁺(O)-CO turns into once H₂ reaches the surface. This is the carbonyl the paper's RWGS plus CO-hydrogenation route runs through, so its presence under reaction rather than under a CO probe is the point of the measurement. Literature values quoted alongside it are 2166 to 2173 cm⁻¹.

Table S5: assigned to Cu²⁺-CO, against a literature value of 2199 cm⁻¹. The table lists its feed condition as CO₂+H₂, but the only figures showing the band are the formic acid and methanol adsorption experiments over Cu/SiO₂ (Figs. S15a and S16a), so the table and the figures do not agree on which experiment it came from and the sample is recorded as the one those figures name. A Cu²⁺ carbonyl on a catalyst reduced at 300 °C is a minority claim, and the paper neither argues it further nor uses it.

Monocarbonyl Cu⁺-CO in a Cu-exchanged zeolite, resolved by self-supporting-pellet transmission FTIR (100 K) into 4 distinct Cu⁺ site sub-families: 2166 cm⁻¹ (most electrophilic cationic site, preferentially covered by co-adsorbed H₂O), 2158 cm⁻¹ (principal/dominant cationic site), 2141 cm⁻¹ (a more highly-coordinated, oxide-like Cu⁺ site), and 2139 cm⁻¹ (Cu⁺(H₂O)(CO) mixed-ligand complex, nearly coincident with the oxide-like site). Site assignment supported by selective monocarbonyl→dicarbonyl→tricarbonyl conversion as CO coverage increases/temperature decreases — see co_gemdi_asym/co_gemdi_sym for the dicarbonyl stage.

C-bonded (X⁺···CO) carbon monoxide on alkali-exchanged and protonic ZSM-5 zeolites (Si/Al = 14), assigned by transmission FTIR at 77 K. Position correlates linearly with 1/(R(M)+R(CO))² (R(M) = cation ionic radius), confirming a purely electrostatic, non-backdonating interaction — unlike the π-backdonating metallic-surface picture elsewhere in this dataset. High-frequency (HF) band positions at low CO coverage: Li⁺ 2188, Na⁺ 2178, K⁺ 2166, Rb⁺ 2162, Cs⁺ 2157, H⁺ (Brønsted) 2172 cm⁻¹ — frequency decreases monotonically with increasing cation radius/decreasing Lewis acidity. Each cation's HF band is accompanied by a much weaker low-frequency (LF) shoulder assigned to the O-bonded isomer of the same adduct, in thermodynamic equilibrium with this C-bonded form — see co_isocarbonyl.

bands.description: CO coordinated through its oxygen rather than its carbon, the reverse orientation of every other CO band here. On an electrostatic cation site with no backdonation the field polarises the bond the other way, so O-bonding puts ν(CO) below the free-gas value while C-bonding on the same site puts it above. The two orientations coexist as close-lying isomers, with the C-bonded one preferred and far stronger.

references.note: O-bonded (X⁺···OC) isocarbonyl species on the same alkali-exchanged and protonic ZSM-5 zeolites as co_cation_stretch's HF band, in thermodynamic equilibrium with it: B3-LYP calculations on naked cations predict O-bonding is only slightly less stable than C-bonding, the energy gap narrowing from Li⁺ to Cs⁺, and a red-shifted shoulder consistent with that prediction is observed for every cation. Low-frequency (LF) band positions: Li⁺ 2108, Na⁺ 2113, K⁺ 2117, Rb⁺ 2119, Cs⁺ 2122, H⁺ (Brønsted) 2115 cm⁻¹ — frequency rises (shifts less below the free-gas 2143 cm⁻¹ value) with increasing cation radius, mirroring the HF band's opposite trend. Relative intensity of this band to the HF band (A(HF)/A(LF)) drops markedly from Li⁺ to Cs⁺, consistent with the two states' energies converging.

bands.description: Asymmetric ν(CO) component of a geminal dicarbonyl species: two linear CO ligands bound to a single isolated cationic metal center, stretching out of phase (one lengthens as the other shortens). The symmetric/asymmetric pair appearing together, rather than a single linear-CO band, is itself diagnostic of an atomically dispersed cationic site — a single metal atom isolated enough to bind two CO molecules at once. Typical splitting between the pair is ~50–60 cm⁻¹.

references.note: νₐₛ(CO) of Cu⁺(CO)₂ geminal dicarbonyl in a Cu-exchanged zeolite at 2151 cm⁻¹ (paired with νₛ at 2180, see co_gemdi_sym), forming from the monocarbonyl with increasing CO coverage. The geminal (one-cation-two-CO) assignment was proven unambiguously by adsorbing a 1:1 ¹²CO+¹³CO isotopic mixture: a force-field calculation from the pure-¹²CO dicarbonyl frequencies predicted mixed-isotope Cu⁺(¹²CO)(¹³CO) bands at 2169/2113 cm⁻¹ and Cu⁺(¹³CO)₂ bands at 2131/2103 cm⁻¹, and both were observed exactly as calculated — only explainable if two CO ligands genuinely share one cation and vibrationally couple, ruling out two coincidentally-overlapping monocarbonyl bands from different sites.

bands.description: Symmetric ν(CO) component of geminal dicarbonyl species with two linear CO ligands bound to a single isolated cationic metal center. Appears together with the asymmetric band and is characteristic of isolated cationic adsorption sites.

references.note: νₛ(CO) of Cu⁺(CO)₂ geminal dicarbonyl in a Cu-exchanged zeolite at 2180 cm⁻¹ (paired with νₐₛ at 2151, see co_gemdi_asym for the ¹²CO/¹³CO isotopic-mixture proof of the geminal assignment). At low temperature, a further conversion to Cu⁺(CO)₃ tricarbonyl was observed (bands at 2190/2164/2140 cm⁻¹, not separately modeled in this dataset).

bands.description: Surface formyl C=O stretch (HCO*); mechanistic intermediate from CO + H. Often observed transiently. Distinguishes the CO-H pathway from formate-mediated routes.

references.note: Table 3 and Fig. 3B, 30 bar. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. ν(C=O) at 1759 cm⁻¹, assigned either to formyl *HCO or to *HCOOH held by a weak hydrogen bond, the small red shift from gaseous HC(=O)OH at 1776 cm⁻¹ being the argument for the latter. One of four bands (1759, 1691, 1457 and 1398 cm⁻¹) whose intensity rises with the GHSV and with the methanol in the outlet gas, which is this paper’s criterion for a true intermediate rather than a spectator. Absent under a 2H₂/CO feed, where no adsorbate could be identified between 2400 and 2000 cm⁻¹ at all.

bands.description: Formyl C-H stretch (HCO*); lower than formate ν(CH) at ~2870-2900 and weaker. Diagnostic when paired with C=O at ~1750.
Adsorbed formaldehyde C=O stretch (H₂CO*); reduction product of formyl. Key methanol precursor in some mechanisms.
Adsorbed formaldehyde CH₂ asymmetric stretch (H₂CO*).
Adsorbed formaldehyde CH₂ symmetric stretch (H₂CO*).
Adsorbed formaldehyde CH₂ scissoring (H₂CO*); overlaps monodentate carbonate νₐₛ.
Generic surface acyl/aldehyde C=O stretch (R-C=O*); broad assignment used when species cannot be specifically identified. Distinguishes from formate by absence of ν(CH) at ~2870.

C=O stretch of formic acid adsorbed without losing its proton. It is the one band that tells molecular HCOOH* from the formate it becomes: formate has no localised carbonyl, its two C-O bonds being equivalent, so nothing of its own absorbs here. An absorption in this window after dosing formic acid therefore means the acid did not fully dissociate, and its disappearance on warming tracks the deprotonation. It sits among the surface carbonyl and carbonate bands, which is the standing ambiguity where the acid was not deliberately dosed.

references.note: Table 1 and Fig. 6b, 6f (IRRAS, UHV, room temperature): a band absent from the group's earlier unpolarized work, strong in s-polarized light and much weaker in p, which puts the C=O bond tilted rather than flat. DFT for a monodentate molecular species gives 1721 cm⁻¹. It is the paper's evidence that formic acid adsorbs monodentate and undissociated alongside the formate on this facet. Nothing equivalent appears on Fe₃O₄(001) at room temperature, where a 1700 cm⁻¹ band was seen only at 190 K in earlier work.

bands.description: Hydroxymethyl O-H stretch (H₂COH*); late methanol precursor. Often masked by surface OH.
Hydroxymethyl CH₂ stretch (H₂COH*); overlaps methoxy and methanol.
Hydroxymethyl C-O stretch (H₂COH*); overlaps methoxy ν(C-O) at ~1050-1100.

C-H stretch of methylenebisoxy (dioxymethylene), the intermediate between formate and formaldehyde with both oxygens still bound to the surface. It lands within about ten wavenumbers of formate's own ν(CH), and on catalysts where formate shows a Fermi doublet the lower arm of that doublet sits here too, so position alone cannot separate them. What identifies it is a temperature or transient profile of its own, out of step with the formate it comes from. Assignments rest on calculated frequencies rather than a reference spectrum, since the species cannot be dosed.

bands.description: Asymmetric OCO stretch of polydentate carbonate: a carbonate bound through more than two oxygens, or bridging several cations, typically built into the top layer of a basic oxide rather than sitting on it. It overlaps the monodentate νₐₛ band and the bottom of the bidentate one, and its splitting from the symmetric partner falls between theirs, so position and spacing alone rarely identify it. What does is stability: polydentate carbonate outlasts the other two on heating and under hydrogen. No binding-geometry field is set, because the carbonate vibration-modes page has only monodentate and bidentate forms so far.

bands.description: Symmetric OCO stretch of polydentate carbonate, the partner of νₐₛ(OCO) p-CO₃²⁻. It lands in the same window as the bidentate symmetric stretch and on top of formate's, so it is the less useful of the pair: the two carbonates are told apart by their asymmetric partners and by how long they survive heating, not here.

Lower-frequency member of the split degenerate pair (the out-of-phase counterpart is νₐₛ(OCO) at ~1500–1670 cm⁻¹). Rarely reported separately from the higher-frequency modes because it falls in a region also occupied by methoxy ν(CO) and formaldehyde bands.

Distinguishing it from carbonate rests on the COH bend near 1220 cm⁻¹ and on its disappearance under deuteration, since carbonate has no proton to lose.

It sits well below the free surface hydroxyls it forms from, and far above the roughly 2550 cm⁻¹ of the hydrogen-bonded dimer in the bulk salt, so its position also says the adsorbed species is not dimerised. Weak beside the OCO stretches, and it falls inside the hydroxyl envelope of the support, so it is read against the clean surface rather than in an absolute spectrum.

bands.description: The bicarbonate COH bend after exchange with D₂O. It drops by about 250 cm⁻¹, far more than the OCO stretches move, because it is the mode that actually swings the hydrogen. bands.description: Bicarbonate O-H stretch with ¹⁸O on the oxide. It moves by only about 10 cm⁻¹, since the hydrogen carries almost all of the motion and the oxygen mass barely enters it, and it moves by that much whether or not the labelled oxygen is the protonated one. That is the first sign that the oxygen the proton ends up on is not the one it started on.

bands.description: Formate C-H stretch, the key HCOO* marker and strongly site-sensitive across its window: κ²-HCOO* on metallic Cu sits near 2848 to 2860 cm⁻¹ and the same mode on a cation or oxide site 20 to 40 cm⁻¹ higher, far enough to resolve two formate populations in one spectrum. Two traps at the low end: methoxy νₛ(CH₃) on silica and adsorbed methanol νₛ(CH₃) both land there, so a band near 2850 cm⁻¹ is safely formate only once its combination band near 2930 cm⁻¹ or a deuteration check backs it up.
