Cutting the hydrogen stops the reaction at HCOO*, and this band grows while methoxy disappears; restoring H₂ removes it completely (Figs. 5d, 5e). It is not detected at steady state, which the paper puts down to low coverage. Recorded on Cu⁰ rather than on the interface because the position is the same on Cu/SiO₂ and CuGa(0.20), which is the paper's own argument that formate does not sit at the Cu-Ga₂O₃ interface.

Fig. S15a and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, 4% HCOOH/Ar at 20 mL min⁻¹, 220 °C, atmospheric pressure, then swept with Ar for 30 min): the reference experiment behind the assignment above. Formic acid dosed on Cu/SiO₂ makes bidentate formate directly, and its ν(CH) lands 6 cm⁻¹ below the band seen under CO₂ with the hydrogen cut off, close enough that the paper treats the two as the same species.

Fig. 1b (ME-DRIFTS-PSD, Cu-GaZrOₓ, 20 bar, 260 °C, CO₂ modulated at constant H₂): ν(CH) of HCOO* at 2876 cm⁻¹, responding at the modulation frequency, which is what marks it an intermediate rather than a spectator. The same position appears as a weak out-of-phase peak on the Cu-free GaZrOₓ at 1 bar (Fig. 4b inset), where the authors read it as slow reduction of surface (bi)carbonates by Ga-H rather than as the fast Cu-catalysed route.

Fig. S4a, reference spectrum rather than a working catalyst: formate generated on precipitated ZrO₂ by flowing CO over the surface hydroxyls (*OH + CO → HCOO*) at 260 °C and 20 bar. ν(CH) centred near 2859 cm⁻¹, and clearer once H₂ was added to the feed. This is the measurement the paper uses to attribute the catalyst's formate bands to the oxide rather than to Cu.

Fig. S4b, the same CO-dosing reference experiment on precipitated Ga₂O₃ at 260 °C and 20 bar. ν(CH) is a minor peak centred near 2887 cm⁻¹, weaker than on ZrO₂, where the asymmetric OCO region carried most of the formate intensity instead.

Lower arm of the formate ν(CH) Fermi resonance doublet at 2910 cm⁻¹ on CeO₂ (upper arm at 2945 cm⁻¹); ¹³C isotopic shift confirms C-H origin. Formate pool is large but exchanges more slowly than the bidentate carbonate pool, suggesting formate is not the primary RWGS active intermediate.

Operando DRIFTS, 230 °C, 10–20 bar, H₂/CO₂ = 3, Cu–M/SiO₂ from SOMC. MCR-ALS resolves two kinetically distinct κ²-HCOO* components. On metallic Cu (2848–2860 cm⁻¹): Fig. 4a/4c (2856), Fig. 5b (2850) and Fig. 7a (2850/2854); per catalyst in the SI, Fig. S15 2860 and Fig. S18 2852 (Cu/SiO₂), Fig. S16 2850 and Fig. S20 2848 (Cu–Ga/SiO₂), Fig. S17 2858 and Fig. S19 2854 (Cu–In/SiO₂). The first and most abundant surface species over all four catalysts, dominating the time-resolved spectra from the first minutes onward (Fig. S10). Exchanges to κ²-DCOO* within the 10 s acquisition limit under D₂, so formate formation and exchange are not rate-limiting; on Cu it is also the RWGS intermediate, its decay tracking the rise of CO* at 2108–2115 cm⁻¹. On the isolated cationic promoter (2877–2896 cm⁻¹): clean only on Zn²⁺ (2896); on Ga³⁺ (2881–2883, Figs. S16/S20) and In³⁺ (2877, Fig. S19) the component is non-separable from Cu-bound formate and methoxy. Formate reaches the promoter by spillover from Cu, not by CO₂ activation on the promoter itself — isolated M/SiO₂ without Cu converts no CO₂ at all.

H₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S13 inset and Table S2; the same band appears in Fig. 5a under CO₂/H₂ = 1:3, and at 2898 cm⁻¹ in Fig. 4c, where CO₂ is dosed onto a pre-formed Ga-H surface at 200 °C). Weak beside the 1581 cm⁻¹ OCO band of the same formate: on this oxide the C-H stretch is a minor feature, which is why it is easy to miss on Ga-containing catalysts. Fig. 4c is the cleanest of the three, since there the formate can only have come from the hydride.

Fig. 7a, 7c, 7e (IRRAS, UHV, room temperature): four C-H stretching bands resolved, of which three are formate. 2868 cm⁻¹ shows only in p-polarized light and marks the upright bidentate species on tetrahedral-Fe sites; 2848 and 2917 cm⁻¹ appear in s-polarized light and belong to flatter formate on interstitial sites. The paper notes how rarely the C-H stretch of formate is reported at all by this technique, its dipole change being much smaller than that of the OCO stretches.

Fig. 7b, 7d, 7f (IRRAS, UHV, room temperature): only three C-H bands here and the 2868 cm⁻¹ one is missing. Its absence is the argument: 2868 cm⁻¹ marked the upright bidentate-bridging species, which this facet cannot host, so the C-H region independently confirms what the OCO stretches say about geometry.

Figs. 6a, S56g and S56h (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar; H₂ step for 30ZnHfOₓ, H₂:CO₂:N₂ = 3:1:1 for the others): formate ν(CH) at 2887 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ, 2892 cm⁻¹ on 20ZnHfOₓ and 2894 cm⁻¹ on 90ZnHfOₓ, labelled νₛ(C–H) in the paper. The near-identity of 20 and 90ZnHfOₓ, against 2873 cm⁻¹ on ZnO, is its argument that both kinds of catalyst hold formate at the same Zn–Vₒ–Hf motif.

Figs. 8e and S56i (operando DRIFTS, ZnO reference, 320 °C, 20 bar, H₂:CO₂:N₂ = 3:1:1): formate on the Hf-free oxide at about 2873 cm⁻¹, some 20 cm⁻¹ below the ZnHfOₓ catalysts and in line with earlier formic-acid dosing on ZnO that the paper cites. Weak: ZnO activates CO₂ poorly, and only very weak methoxy bands form alongside.

Fig. 8e and Section 2.9 (operando DRIFTS, bare monoclinic HfO₂ reference, 90 min at 320 °C, 20 bar, H₂:CO₂:N₂ = 3:1:1): formate forms on the Zn-free oxide, weaker than on 30ZnHfOₓ, although no methanol leaves the cell. The paper prints no position, only that the 30ZnHfOₓ band sits 4 to 5 cm⁻¹ lower, between HfO₂ and ZnO; that in-between position is its case for an intermediate bound at a site involving both Zn and Hf. No value is recorded: the figure is not labelled with one.

bands.description: Formate asymmetric OCO stretch, the marker band of HCOO* and usually the stronger of the two OCO stretches. Its position is not fixed: it moves with the adsorption geometry, so read it together with the symmetric partner and the Δν between them rather than on its own. The in-phase and antiphase C-O pair is what separates formate from carbonate and carboxylate features.

references.note: Table 2/Fig. 1a (Ru/Al₂O₃) and Fig. 3a (Ru–6.1%"Na₂O"/Al₂O₃ DFM): νas(OCO) HCOO* at 1520 cm⁻¹ on both surfaces, appearing at the onset of H₂ reduction (methanation step, 320 °C, 20% H₂/N₂). On Ru/Al₂O₃, formate forms via spillover of bicarbonates (adsorbed on Al₂O₃ OH groups); on Ru–Na₂O/Al₂O₃, it forms after bidentate carbonates (on Al-O⁻-Na⁺ sites) spill over to the Ru–support interface — same position despite the different CO₂ adsorption pathway. Confirmed reaction intermediate en route to CH₄.

Fig. 1b (ME-DRIFTS-PSD, Cu-GaZrOₓ, 20 bar, 260 °C): νₐₛ(OCO) of HCOO* at 1600 cm⁻¹, responding at the modulation frequency of the CO₂ feed. Methanol steam reforming over the same sample at 1 bar puts the band at 1590 cm⁻¹ and shows it only while CO₂(g) is formed (Fig. 2b), which is the reverse-direction evidence for the same intermediate. On the Cu-free GaZrOₓ the peaks between 1250 and 1700 cm⁻¹ are assigned to carbonates and bicarbonates instead, so this position is not by itself proof of formate.

Fig. S4a, formate generated on precipitated ZrO₂ from CO and surface hydroxyls at 260 °C and 20 bar. The paper quotes the asymmetric OCO vibrations as lying between 1582 and 1641 cm⁻¹; only the 1582 cm⁻¹ component is recorded here, because the upper end of that range overlaps the carbonate and bicarbonate bands the same dosing experiment produces (Fig. S3) and the paper does not separate them.
Table 3: νas(OCO⁻) at 1585 cm⁻¹; dominant CH₄ adsorption product on Al₂O₃ via H-abstraction; nearly absent on La-modified and Ni-Ce-Fe/La-Al₂O₃ under DRM.

Table 3 and Fig. 3. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. νₐₛ(OCO) at 1587 cm⁻¹ at 1 bar and 1603 cm⁻¹ at 30 bar, assigned to bidentate and to unidentate formate respectively. The splittings against νₛ agree with that split rather than contradict it: 227 cm⁻¹ for the 1 bar pair and 289 cm⁻¹ for the 30 bar pair, and a carboxylate bound through one oxygen splits wider than one chelating through both. The 30 bar formate is this paper’s spectator: strong, but its intensity does not follow the GHSV, it is still there on the catalytically inactive CZ-2000, and hours of H₂ flushing are needed to remove it.

Fig. 7a (MCR-resolved, He+CO₂ vs H₂+He switching, 230 °C, 20 bar, Cu–Zn/SiO₂): νₐₛ(C–O) of κ²-HCOO* at 1590 cm⁻¹, resolved alongside the same component's ν(C–H) at 2850 cm⁻¹ so the C–H and C–O regions can be cross-checked against one MCR component rather than assigned separately. Fig. S19 in the SI gives 1544 cm⁻¹ for the same species on Cu–In/SiO₂ — some 46 cm⁻¹ lower, the same direction the promoter shifts every other formate band here. Fig. 6a plots this frequency (for the deuterated κ²-DCOO* form) against intrinsic CH₃OH formation rate as a Sabatier volcano spanning roughly 1530–1600 cm⁻¹ across the four catalysts, weaker C–O binding on the right; the per-catalyst values behind that plot are not tabulated.

H₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S13, and Fig. 5b under CO₂/H₂ = 1:3 from 30 to 450 °C): introducing H₂ converts the carbonates into formate, which appears as a single dominant band at 1581 cm⁻¹ and grows from about 200 °C, the same temperature at which the Ga-H hydride becomes mobile. On this Cu-free oxide the formate is made by the hydride rather than by a metal. Fig. S12 shows the same conversion isothermally at 300 °C, where H₂ purging turns the carbonate bands into this one.

Table 1 and Fig. 6 (IRRAS, UHV, room temperature): νₐₛ(OCO) of bidentate-bridging formate. The 1555 cm⁻¹ band appears only in p-polarized light and is the paper's headline result, the first direct observation of this stretch for formate on an octahedral Fe site with a tetrahedral Fe underneath. The companion at 1548 cm⁻¹ belongs to the interstitial-site species and shows at 1538 cm⁻¹ in s-polarized light. Both are positive in absorbance, the opposite sign to the symmetric stretch, which places their dipole parallel to the surface.

Table 1 and Fig. 6 (IRRAS, UHV, room temperature): νₐₛ(OCO) at 1588 cm⁻¹ for the quasi-bidentate species and 1548 cm⁻¹, very weak, for the chelating one. Pairing each with its symmetric partner gives splittings of 253 and 168 cm⁻¹: the chelating geometry has the smaller O-C-O angle and the smaller splitting, which is the standard geometry diagnostic recovered here from polarization rather than from position alone.

Figs. 6a to 6c (operando DRIFTS, 30ZnHfOₓ, 320 °C, 20 bar, switching 20 vol% CO₂ → 80 vol% H₂ → H₂:CO₂:N₂ = 3:1:1, all in N₂): the dominant formate band, which the paper calls ν(C=O). It appears the instant H₂ replaces CO₂ and fades as methoxy grows; re-admitting CO₂ restores it at once while methoxy falls, the formate-methoxy pathway read straight off the spectra. The site is the paper's postulate: the formate and methoxy bands on 30ZnHfOₓ sit 4 to 5 cm⁻¹ below those on HfO₂ and between the two single oxides (Fig. 8e), which it reads as stabilisation at a Zn–Vₒ–Hf motif. Fig. S49 repeats the sequence on 20ZnHfOₓ with the same result; its caption repeats Fig. 6's tracking positions word for word, so it is not recorded as a separate 20ZnHfOₓ position.

bands.description: Formate symmetric OCO stretch (HCOO*), paired with νₐₛ(OCO) above. The splitting Δν = νₐₛ − νₛ between the two paired bands is a standard diagnostic for adsorption geometry — how it compares between a more bridging-like and a more chelating-like coordination is a recurring theme in formate vibrational assignments. Where multiple coordination geometries coexist and overlap, polarization-dependent IRRAS/DRIFTS can resolve components that look like a single broad feature in an unpolarized spectrum.

references.note: Table 2/Fig. 1a (Ru/Al₂O₃) and Fig. 3a (Ru–6.1%"Na₂O"/Al₂O₃ DFM): νₛ(OCO) HCOO* at 1320 cm⁻¹ on both surfaces, paired with νas at 1520 cm⁻¹; appears at onset of H₂ reduction (320 °C, 20% H₂/N₂). On Ru/Al₂O₃, formate forms via bicarbonate spillover at the Ru–Al₂O₃ interface; on Ru–Na₂O/Al₂O₃, from bidentate carbonate spillover to the Ru–support interface. Identified as a key CO₂ methanation intermediate.

Table 1 and Figs. 6a, 6c (p-polarized IRRAS, UHV, formic acid dosed at room temperature): bidentate-bridging formate resolved into two components, 1369 cm⁻¹ on an Fe site with a tetrahedral Fe underneath and 1377 cm⁻¹ on one with an interstitial Fe. Both are negative Fano features in p-polarized light, which places their transition dipole perpendicular to the surface and stands the formate upright. Unpolarized light cannot separate the two, and this is the first time they were told apart experimentally rather than by calculation.

Table 1 and Figs. 6b, 6d (p-polarized IRRAS, UHV, room temperature): two geometries on the other facet, quasi-bidentate at 1335 cm⁻¹ and chelating at 1380 cm⁻¹, fitted as two separate Fano components (Fig. 8c). Bidentate bridging is absent here: the tetrahedral Fe atoms sit 5.9 Å apart, too far for one formate to span. Chelating forms first, visible from 0.05 L, and the quasi-bidentate species only appears above 0.2 L, once hydrogen from the dissociation has covered the oxygen-terminated patches.
Fig. 1b (ME-DRIFTS-PSD, Cu-GaZrOₓ, 20 bar, 260 °C): νₛ(OCO) marked at 1350 cm⁻¹, the companion of the 1600 cm⁻¹ asymmetric band and modulating with it.

Fig. S4a, formate generated on precipitated ZrO₂ from CO and surface hydroxyls at 260 °C and 20 bar. The paper reports symmetric OCO vibrations centred near 1290 and 1381 cm⁻¹; the 1381 cm⁻¹ component is recorded here, since 1290 cm⁻¹ sits in the carbonate region of the same spectrum and the paper does not say which species it belongs to.
Table 3: νs(OCO⁻) at 1380 cm⁻¹.

Table 3 and Fig. 3. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. νₛ(OCO) at 1360 cm⁻¹ at 1 bar, bidentate, and 1314 cm⁻¹ at 30 bar, unidentate, the partners of νₐₛ at 1587 and 1603 cm⁻¹. See that entry for the spectator argument. Literature values cited: 1363, 1352, 1360 and 1363 cm⁻¹ for the first, 1352 and 1357 cm⁻¹ for the second.

H₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S13; also Fig. 5b under CO₂/H₂ = 1:3 from 30 to 450 °C): the lower of the two weak formate components below the dominant 1581 cm⁻¹ band. Fig. S13 marks both HCOO* without saying which is which, but Table S2 separates them, νₛ(OCO) at 1370 cm⁻¹ and δ(CH) at 1386 cm⁻¹, so the two are recorded as separate claims rather than as one pair on this band.

Fig. 6a (30ZnHfOₓ, H₂ and H₂:CO₂ steps, 320 °C, 20 bar): a band labelled HCOO* in the figure and not discussed in the text, which names no mode for it. It is recorded here because νₛ(OCO) is what this position and its 207 cm⁻¹ splitting from 1578 cm⁻¹ point to, but δ(CH) lands in the same place and the paper does not separate them. Zn–Vₒ–Hf is the paper's postulated site for all its intermediates (Section 2.9, Fig. 8e).

bands.description: Formate C-H bending (HCOO*); overlaps νₛ(OCO).

references.note: Not resolved separately: on Cu-GaZrOₓ at 20 bar and 260 °C the C-H bend falls under the νₛ(OCO) feature marked at 1350 cm⁻¹, and the paper treats the 1350 to 1400 cm⁻¹ region as one formate signal. Recorded without a wavenumber because the paper gives none for this mode alone.

Table 3 and Fig. 3B, 30 bar. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. δ(CH) of unidentate formate at 1371 cm⁻¹, the middle band of the 1603/1371/1314 cm⁻¹ set that appears together and behaves as one species. Literature values cited: 1370 and 1375 cm⁻¹.

H₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S13; Table S2): δ(CH) of HCOO*, the upper of the two weak formate components below the dominant 1581 cm⁻¹ band and 16 cm⁻¹ above its νₛ(OCO) partner. Both are minor features on this Cu-free oxide, where formate is read almost entirely from the asymmetric OCO stretch. The same bend carries the two formate combination bands of Table S2, and 1386 + 1370 reproduces the observed 2757 cm⁻¹ exactly, which is what fixes this assignment against the νₛ(OCO) it overlaps.

Table 1 and Fig. 8a (IRRAS, UHV, room temperature): δ(CH) of bidentate-bridging formate, at 1373 cm⁻¹ in p-polarized and 1385 cm⁻¹ in s-polarized light. Its Fano line shape is inverted relative to the symmetric OCO stretch that sits almost on top of it, and that sign difference, not the position, is what separates the two. The paper reads the pair of polarizations as a C-H bond that is tilted rather than upright.

Table 1 (IRRAS, UHV, room temperature): δ(CH) at 1385 cm⁻¹ for the quasi-bidentate species and 1280 cm⁻¹ for the chelating one, both seen in s-polarized light. The 105 cm⁻¹ between them is far larger than this mode usually moves, and 1280 cm⁻¹ is the lowest position this atlas holds for a formate C-H bend, so the band window is stretched to reach it on the strength of one polarization-resolved study.

bands.description: Formate combination band (HCOO*): bending + asymmetric stretch; diagnostic for HCOO*. Runs low enough on cationic-promoted Cu (~2923 cm⁻¹) to sit right on top of methoxy νₐₛ(CH₃) — the two are told apart by deuteration, which moves this combination out of the C-H region altogether while methoxy's own fundamental simply shifts down to its C-D position.

references.note: Figs. 5b, 5c and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, 220 °C, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹, switching H₂/CO₂ 3/1 → He/CO₂ 3/1): δ(CH)+νₐₛ(OCO) of bidentate formate, rising with ν(CH) at 2890 cm⁻¹ when the hydrogen is cut and vanishing when it returns. Dosing formic acid directly on Cu/SiO₂ puts the same combination at the same 2956 cm⁻¹ (Fig. S15a), which is what ties the two experiments together. The position is unchanged between Cu/SiO₂ and CuGa(0.20), the paper's argument that this formate is on Cu⁰ and not at the Cu-Ga₂O₃ interface.

Upper arm of the formate ν(CH) Fermi resonance doublet at 2945 cm⁻¹ on CeO₂ (lower arm at 2910 cm⁻¹). The ~35 cm⁻¹ doublet splitting is characteristic of HCOO* Fermi coupling between ν(CH) and 2δ(CH) or δ(OCH)+νₐₛ(OCO).

Fig. 4a/4c and Fig. 7a (operando DRIFTS, 230 °C, 10–20 bar, H₂/CO₂ = 3, Cu–M/SiO₂ from SOMC): explicitly assigned as ν(C–O)+δ(C–H) of κ²-HCOO* on Cu⁰ and paired with ν(CH) at 2850–2856 cm⁻¹. MCR-resolved per catalyst in the SI: Fig. S15 2929 cm⁻¹ (Cu/SiO₂), Fig. S16 2923 cm⁻¹ (Cu–Ga/SiO₂), Fig. S17 2937 cm⁻¹ (Cu–In/SiO₂), Fig. S19 2933 cm⁻¹, Fig. S18 2931 cm⁻¹, Fig. S20 2929 cm⁻¹ — a ~14 cm⁻¹ spread tracking the promoter's electron-withdrawing effect on the formate C–O bond. Deuteration is what proves the combination character: under D₂ this feature leaves the C–H region entirely, while the genuine ν(C–D) fundamental appears at 2161–2184 cm⁻¹, which is precisely why the SSITKA C–D window is the clean one for reading out formate bond strengths.

H₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S13 inset, and Fig. 5a under CO₂/H₂ = 1:3 from 30 to 450 °C; Table S2): δ(CH)+νₐₛ(OCO) of HCOO*, the highest of the three formate features in the C-H window and well clear of ν(CH) at 2897 cm⁻¹. The fundamentals the same table reports sum to 2967 cm⁻¹, about 12 cm⁻¹ below the observed band. Its lower counterpart δ(CH)+νₛ(OCO) is also resolved here, at 2757 cm⁻¹, which is unusual: most sources report only this upper one.

Fig. 7 and Table 1 (IRRAS, UHV, room temperature): assigned as a coupling of the asymmetric OCO stretch with the C-H bend, and seen on both magnetite facets at the same position. It appears in p-polarized light on Fe₃O₄(001). Recorded here rather than as a C-H fundamental because the paper treats it as the combination, consistent with the earlier assignment of a band near 2950 cm⁻¹ on Cu(110).

Fig. 6a (30ZnHfOₓ, H₂ step, 320 °C, 20 bar): the weaker partner of the 2887 cm⁻¹ band, assigned in the paper as νₐₛ(C–H) of formate against νₛ(C–H) at 2887 cm⁻¹. Formate has a single C–H bond and so no symmetric and asymmetric pair; the atlas files this band as the δ(CH)+νₐₛ(OCO) combination its position matches, and the νₐₛ(C–H) label is the paper's.

bands.description: Formate combination band: the C-H bend plus the symmetric OCO stretch, and the lower partner of the δ(OCH)+νₐₛ(OCO) combination near 2950 cm⁻¹. A weak band on each side of ν(CH) is the signature the pair provides, since neither carbonate nor methoxy produces one. This is the weaker of the two and the easier to lose in a sloping baseline, so it is reported far less often than its partner. Its position is arithmetic rather than chemistry: it follows whatever the two fundamentals do, so a change in the OCO splitting between sites moves this band and its partner in opposite directions.

references.note: Fig. 5a (operando DRIFTS, precipitated Ga₂O₃, CO₂/H₂ = 1:3, 30 to 450 °C; Table S2): δ(CH)+νₛ(OCO) of HCOO*, the lowest of the three formate features in the C-H window. The two fundamentals the same table gives, 1386 and 1370 cm⁻¹, sum to 2756 cm⁻¹, one wavenumber off the observed band, which is a tighter match than the upper combination manages and is what makes this the cleaner of the pair to argue from here.

Fig. S15a and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, 4% HCOOH/Ar at 20 mL min⁻¹, 220 °C, atmospheric pressure): δ(CH)+νₛ(OCO) of bidentate formate made by dosing formic acid on Cu/SiO₂. The paper marks it as its own result with no literature value to cite, which fits how rarely this lower combination is reported next to its partner at 2956 cm⁻¹. Seen only in the formic acid experiment: it does not appear under CO₂ and H₂, where formate is below the detection limit at steady state.

bands.description: C-D stretch of κ²-DCOO*, the deuterated twin of ν(CH) HCOO* and red-shifted from it by the 0.73 mass factor. Site-sensitive in the same way: formate on metallic Cu sits 15 to 20 cm⁻¹ below formate on a cation site. Deuteration is what makes this window readable, moving the δ(OCH)+νₐₛ(OCO) combination out of the way and leaving one uncluttered fundamental. Two overlaps: gas-phase CO's R branch sits on top of it, and deuterated methoxy brackets it, with νₛ(CD₃) just below the window and νₐₛ(CD₃) at its top.

references.note: Fig. 5b (MCR-resolved, Cu–Zn/SiO₂ SSITKA, CO₂+D₂ ⇄ CO₂+H₂, 230 °C, 10 bar, D₂ or H₂/CO₂ = 3): κ²-DCOO*(Cu) at 2167 cm⁻¹. Per catalyst in the SI: Fig. S15 2161 cm⁻¹ (Cu/SiO₂), Fig. S16 2176 cm⁻¹ (Cu–Ga/SiO₂), Fig. S17 2169 cm⁻¹ (Cu–In/SiO₂). Fig. 6b plots those four points and uses 2173 cm⁻¹ for Cu–Zn/SiO₂ — the Gaussian-fitted centre of the overlapping Cu⁰ and Zn²⁺ components, not a separate species; across Cu/SiO₂ → Cu–In → Cu–Zn → Cu–Ga the ν(C–D) frequency rises monotonically and intrinsic CH₃OH selectivity rises linearly with it (R² > 0.99), making the position a quantitative selectivity descriptor. SI section 1.5.5 derives the expected ν(C–D)/ν(C–H) ratio of ≈0.734 from the harmonic-oscillator reduced masses and uses it to assign this region; Fig. S14 shows the exchange with κ²-HCOO* completes in under 1 min at both switches, so the kinetic isotope effect on formate hydrogenation is negligible.

Fig. 5b (same MCR-resolved Cu–Zn/SiO₂ SSITKA experiment, 230 °C, 10 bar): κ²-DCOO*(Zn²⁺) at 2184 cm⁻¹, kinetically indistinguishable from κ²-DCOO*(Cu) at 2167 cm⁻¹ but spectrally separate — direct evidence that Zn²⁺ supplies a second, distinct Lewis-acid site for formate and simultaneously perturbs the formate on the adjacent Cu. Not resolved for Ga³⁺ or In³⁺ in this region (Figs. S16/S17), where the promoter-bound component overlaps κ²-DCOO*(Cu) or is too dilute at steady state.

bands.description: Asymmetric OCO stretch of deuterated formate. The OCO frame carries almost none of the hydrogen's motion, so this band moves by ten wavenumbers or so rather than by the mass factor that drags ν(CH) down to 2160 cm⁻¹. That near-invariance is the useful part: a band in this window that stays put under D₂ while the C-H window empties is the OCO stretch and nothing else. It remains the strongest formate feature under deuterium, so a deuterated spectrum still reads as formate here.

references.note: D₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S14): DCOO* made by the surface Ga-D, and the dominant band of the spectrum exactly as its protiated twin is at 1581 cm⁻¹ under H₂ (Fig. S13). Deuteration moves it up by 11 cm⁻¹, which is the whole shift. The Ga-D that made it is visible at 1429 cm⁻¹ in the same spectrum, so hydride and product are seen together.

bands.description: Symmetric OCO stretch of deuterated formate, the partner of νₐₛ(OCO) DCOO*. Read the two together: the splitting between them is the same geometry diagnostic as on the protiated species, and comparing the pair against its protiated counterpart separates a real change of binding from the isotope shift. Deuteration is what clears this window, since δ(OCH) near 1380 cm⁻¹ moves away and leaves the symmetric stretch alone where the two normally sit on top of each other.

references.note: D₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S14): the weak lower partner of the 1592 cm⁻¹ band. It sits 29 cm⁻¹ below the 1370 cm⁻¹ νₛ(OCO) the same group reports for HCOO* under H₂, a larger move than the asymmetric partner makes. The δ(CH) at 1386 cm⁻¹ that crowds this region under H₂ is gone, which is why the deuterated spectrum shows one component here where the protiated one shows two.

bands.description: Methoxy CH₃ asymmetric stretch, one C-H bond moving out of phase with the other two. It tracks νₛ(CH₃) below, so a shift in both is a sign that the binding environment itself has changed. Coadsorbed methanol sits a little higher and is easily read as the same species. Silica is the outlier among supports: methoxy grafted as Si-O-CH₃ absorbs near 2955 to 2960 cm⁻¹, some 30 cm⁻¹ above the same mode on Cu.

references.note: Monodentate CH₃O* from CH₃OH dosing on anatase TiO₂.

Figs. 5a, 5c, S17b and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, CuGa(0.20), 220 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): νₐₛ(CH₃) of CH₃O* at steady state, 7 cm⁻¹ below the same mode on the unpromoted Cu/SiO₂. Methoxy is the most abundant surface intermediate here, and that shift is the paper's evidence that on the promoted catalyst it sits on the Cu⁺ site at the Cu-Ga₂O₃ interface rather than on Cu⁰ — an inference from the frequency, since the two catalysts are otherwise alike. Formate is not detected under these conditions.

Figs. 5a, 5b, S17a and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, unpromoted Cu/SiO₂, 220 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): νₐₛ(CH₃) of CH₃O* on the Ga-free reference catalyst, the counterpart of the 2919 cm⁻¹ band on CuGa(0.20). Two claims rather than one pair, because the 7 cm⁻¹ between them is the observation the paper's site argument rests on. It holds its position from 220 to 280 °C (Fig. S17a).

Fig. S16a and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, 10% CH₃OH/Ar at 20 mL min⁻¹, 220 °C, atmospheric pressure, then swept with Ar): νₐₛ(CH₃) of the methoxy left after dosing methanol on Cu/SiO₂ and removing the physisorbed layer. This is the reference experiment that verifies the methoxy assignment under reaction. It sits 28 cm⁻¹ above the band measured under CO₂ and H₂ on the same catalyst, which the paper does not comment on; the value is close to where methoxy grafted onto silica is usually reported.

Fig. 1b (ME-DRIFTS-PSD, Cu-GaZrOₓ, 20 bar, 260 °C): the C-H stretching region of CH₃O* is marked at 2970, 2876 and 2819 cm⁻¹, with 2876 cm⁻¹ belonging to formate. The paper names no site for the methoxy on the catalyst; its own reference spectra on precipitated ZrO₂ and Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S5) are what support reading it as bound to the oxide rather than to Cu.

Fig. 4a/4c (2958 cm⁻¹) and Fig. 7a (2956 cm⁻¹) — operando DRIFTS, 230 °C, 10–20 bar, H₂/CO₂ = 3, Cu–M/SiO₂ from SOMC; MCR-resolved per catalyst in the SI at Fig. S15 2956, Fig. S16 2958, Fig. S18 2952, Fig. S20 2958 cm⁻¹. Methoxy grafted to the silica support (Si-O-CH₃), not to Cu or to the promoter: it builds up slowly (visible only after ~90 min) and, unlike formate, exchanges on the minute-to-hour timescale under D₂. Fig. S14 splits it into a fast, reactive pool near the Cu/promoter interface and a slow (τ ≈ 1 h) spectator pool on remote silica sites — one band, two kinetically distinct populations. The reactive pool's hydrogenation/desorption is the rate-limiting step of the whole cycle (KIE = 2.78), which makes this band a rate proxy rather than a spectator.

Fig. 5a (operando DRIFTS-MS, precipitated Ga₂O₃, CO₂/H₂ = 1:3, 30 to 450 °C; Table S2): νₐₛ(CH₃) of CH₃O*, marked as a shoulder 39 cm⁻¹ below the formate combination band at 2979 cm⁻¹ and paired with νₛ(CH₃) at 2834 cm⁻¹. Methoxy on an oxide carrying no metal at all: it is made from formate by the surface Ga-H hydride, and gas-phase methanol follows it into the mass spectrometer from 304 °C (Fig. S16).

Figs. 6a and 6b (30ZnHfOₓ, H₂ step, 320 °C, 20 bar): νₐₛ(CH₃) of methoxy, growing as formate is hydrogenated under H₂ and falling when CO₂ returns. Zn–Vₒ–Hf is the paper's postulated site: in its DFT, CH₂O* moves to the oxygen vacancy of that motif to be hydrogenated to CH₃O* (Fig. 7).

bands.description: Methoxy CH₃ symmetric stretch (CH₃O*), shifting in tandem with νₐₛ(CH₃) above. Often appears as a close shoulder pair with a coadsorbed methanol band sitting a little higher in frequency. Silica-grafted methoxy is the extreme case, ~2856–2859 cm⁻¹, some 40 cm⁻¹ above the same mode on Cu — high enough that it lands directly on formate's own ν(CH) on metallic Cu (the low end of ν(CH) HCOO*). On a silica-supported Cu catalyst the two are effectively coincident and cannot be separated by position alone.

references.note: Figs. 5a, 5c, S17b and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, CuGa(0.20), 220 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): νₛ(CH₃) of CH₃O* at steady state, the partner of νₐₛ(CH₃) at 2919 cm⁻¹ and shifted from the Ga-free catalyst in the same direction and by a similar amount. That the two CH₃ stretches move together is what makes the shift read as a change of adsorption site rather than as a second species.

Figs. 5a, 5b, S17a and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, unpromoted Cu/SiO₂, 220 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): νₛ(CH₃) of CH₃O* on the Ga-free reference catalyst, paired with νₐₛ(CH₃) at 2926 cm⁻¹. Recorded apart from the CuGa(0.20) value at 2836 cm⁻¹ for the same reason as its partner.

Fig. S16a and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, 10% CH₃OH/Ar at 20 mL min⁻¹, 220 °C, atmospheric pressure, then swept with Ar for 30 min): νₛ(CH₃) of methoxy formed by dosing methanol on Cu/SiO₂, the experiment that verifies the assignment made under reaction. Its partner is at 2954 cm⁻¹. Both sit well above the values the same catalyst gives under CO₂ and H₂, and at this position the band is also where formate's own ν(CH) on metallic Cu is usually found.

Fig. 1b (ME-DRIFTS-PSD, Cu-GaZrOₓ, 20 bar, 260 °C): the lower of the two CH₃O* stretching peaks. The corresponding reference spectra on the single oxides (Fig. S5) put the methoxy C-H stretches between 2797 and 2935 cm⁻¹ without resolving them into symmetric and asymmetric.

Fig. 4a/4c (2858 cm⁻¹) and Fig. 7a (2854 cm⁻¹) — operando DRIFTS, 230 °C, 10–20 bar, H₂/CO₂ = 3, Cu–M/SiO₂ from SOMC; MCR-resolved per catalyst in the SI at Fig. S15 2856, Fig. S16 2858, Fig. S17 2856, Fig. S18 2859, Fig. S20 2858 cm⁻¹. Paired with νₐₛ(CH₃) at 2952–2958 cm⁻¹ in the same MCR component. Under D₂ this fundamental shifts cleanly to 2080 cm⁻¹ (CD₃O*), which is what allows methoxy to be separated from the formate combination band it otherwise overlaps in the C-H region.

H₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S13 inset, and Fig. 5a under CO₂/H₂ = 1:3): the methoxy that formate is converted into as the temperature rises, on an oxide with no metal on it at all. It appears above roughly 250 °C and its growth follows the loss of formate (Fig. 5c). Both figures mark 2837 cm⁻¹, which is the value recorded; Table S2 lists the same band at 2834 cm⁻¹ and names the mode νₛ(CH₃). Its νₐₛ(CH₃) partner is at 2940 cm⁻¹.

Figs. 6a to 6c, S56g and S56h (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar): νₛ(CH₃) of methoxy, the band the paper tracks with time, at 2827 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ, 2832 cm⁻¹ on 20ZnHfOₓ and 2835 cm⁻¹ on 90ZnHfOₓ. After switching to H₂ it grows on every Hf-containing catalyst and markedly less on ZnO, which the paper reads as Hf stabilising methoxy at the Zn–Vₒ–Hf motif.

Figs. 8e, S56i and S56l (ZnO reference, 320 °C, 20 bar, H₂:CO₂:N₂ = 3:1:1 then H₂): methoxy on the Hf-free oxide, very weak, and growing less under H₂ than on the Hf-containing catalysts while formate decreases. Set against the ZnHfOₓ catalysts, this is the paper's evidence that Hf in the active motif is what stabilises methoxy.

Fig. 8e and Section 2.9 (operando DRIFTS, bare monoclinic HfO₂ reference, 90 min at 320 °C, 20 bar, H₂:CO₂:N₂ = 3:1:1): methoxy forms on the Zn-free oxide, weaker than on 30ZnHfOₓ, yet no methanol is detected in the off-gas. The paper suggests slow turnover, or methoxy that cannot be hydrogenated without Zn, which matches the poor H₂ activation of HfO₂ in its H₂-D₂ exchange. No position is printed; the 30ZnHfOₓ band sits 4 to 5 cm⁻¹ lower.

bands.description: Methoxy CH₃ symmetric deformation (CH₃O*) — the methyl "umbrella" mode. Usually the only CH₃-deformation-region band resolved at all, since it's the sole totally-symmetric (A₁) one and therefore the only one with a surface-normal dipole derivative on an ideally perpendicular adsorbate; on real, less rigidly-oriented oxide-supported catalysts it can be unusually weak. Position is comparatively insensitive to binding geometry, unlike the stretches above.

references.note: Table 3: δ(–CH₃) at 1480 cm⁻¹; surface methoxy deformation from CH₄ activation via H-abstraction; observed during DRM at 600°C.

Table 3 and Fig. 3B, 30 bar. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. δ(CH₃) of surface methoxy *H₃CO at 1457 cm⁻¹. Its intensity grows with the catalyst loading in the diluent, alongside the methanol in the outlet gas, and follows the GHSV; that is the paper’s argument both for reading it as methoxy and for calling it an intermediate rather than a spectator. Absent under a 2H₂/CO feed. Literature values cited: 1460, 1445 and 1470 cm⁻¹.

bands.description: Tentatively assigned methoxy CH₃ asymmetric deformation (CH₃O*). Not always separately resolved from δₛ(CH₃) above — some spectra show only the symmetric component. May overlap with formate νₛ(OCO) at ~1365 cm⁻¹, so a band here doesn't necessarily rule out formate also being present.

Monodentate methoxy C-O stretch (CH₃O* bonded via O to a single metal cation). Often resolves into several closely-spaced sub-components rather than one clean peak, reflecting a distribution of slightly different monodentate sites rather than a single uniform one. Diagnostic threshold: ν(C-O) above roughly 1100 cm⁻¹ indicates monodentate geometry, below it bidentate (see methoxy_co_stretch_bi) — the two share the same underlying vibration and just trade off in relative position with coordination number.

references.note: Sub-components at 1100/1126/1156 cm⁻¹ reflecting a distribution of monodentate sites; dominates over bidentate ~3:1 by integrated area; ~1.5× higher photoreactivity toward HCOO* than bidentate.

Fig. 1b (ME-DRIFTS-PSD, Cu-GaZrOₓ, 20 bar, 260 °C): the C-O stretch of CH₃O* at 1152 cm⁻¹, one of the two bands the paper follows through the modulation. It matches the 1154 cm⁻¹ peak of methoxy on precipitated ZrO₂ (Fig. S5), which is the paper's own basis for placing the methoxy on the zirconia rather than on Cu, though it never writes Zr⁴⁺ itself.

Fig. S5, reference spectrum: methanol dosed directly onto precipitated ZrO₂ at 260 °C and 1 bar, with the bubbler then switched off so that only the adsorbed species remain. The paper reports the main C-O stretching peaks at 1111 and 1154 cm⁻¹ and cites Bensitel for the assignment, but does not itself say which peak is the mono- and which the bidentate methoxy. Both are recorded on this band because both fall inside its window.

Fig. 6a (30ZnHfOₓ, H₂ step, 320 °C, 20 bar): terminal methoxy, t-H₃CO*, appearing with the bridged form at 1052 cm⁻¹ as formate is hydrogenated. The paper names the geometry and not the mode; ν(CO) is where the position falls. It tells the two geometries apart by label only and names no site for either beyond its general postulate, Zn–Vₒ–Hf for all its intermediates (Section 2.9, Fig. 8e). Fig. S49 marks both forms on 20ZnHfOₓ in the same switching sequence, without printing positions.

bands.description: Bidentate methoxy C-O stretch (CH₃O* bridging two metal centers, or bonded at a bridging-O vacancy). Diagnostic threshold: ν(C-O) below roughly 1100 cm⁻¹ indicates bidentate geometry (see methoxy_co_stretch_mono for the monodentate counterpart). Overlaps closely with molecular methanol's own ν(C-O) — distinguish via the absence of methanol's own νₛ(CH₃) marker band at higher frequency.

references.note: Similar thermal stability to monodentate (no interconversion ≤ 300 °C); ~1.5× lower photoreactivity toward HCOO* than monodentate.

Fig. S5, reference spectrum: methanol dosed onto precipitated Ga₂O₃ at 260 °C and 1 bar, with the bubbler switched off so only adsorbed species remain. The paper puts the C-O stretch of CH₃O* at 1071 cm⁻¹ on this oxide and gives no binding geometry. It is recorded on the bidentate band because that is where the position falls, not because the paper says so.

Fig. 6a (30ZnHfOₓ, H₂ step, 320 °C, 20 bar): bridged methoxy, b-H₃CO*, the partner of terminal methoxy at 1153 cm⁻¹. The paper names the geometry and not the mode; ν(CO) is where the position falls. Zn–Vₒ–Hf is the paper's postulated site for all its intermediates (Section 2.9, Fig. 8e).

bands.description: CD₃ symmetric stretch of deuterated methoxy, the one methoxy band that survives deuteration as a cleanly resolvable feature. In the ordinary C-H region methoxy overlaps formate's combination band and adsorbed methanol; here it sits about 80 cm⁻¹ clear of the deuterated formate bands and can be integrated on its own. The neighbourhood is crowded in a different way, since CO on reduced metals and CO₂ combination bands absorb here.

references.note: Fig. 5b/5c (MCR-resolved, Cu–Zn/SiO₂ SSITKA, CO₂+D₂ ⇄ CO₂+H₂, 230 °C, 10 bar): CD₃O* on silica at 2080 cm⁻¹, and at exactly the same position on the other three catalysts (SI Figs. S15/S16/S17) — unshifted by the promoter, consistent with methoxy sitting on the silica support rather than at the Cu–promoter interface. Unlike formate, this exchanges slowly, and its concentration profile — not the formate's — tracks the delayed appearance of gas-phase methanol, which is the observation that identifies methoxy hydrogenation/desorption as the rate-limiting step. Fig. S14c/d resolves the decay into a fast reactive pool (τ ≈ 1–6 min) and a slow spectator pool (τ ≈ 55–98 min); Fig. S12 is the linearised fit behind the KIE of 2.78. The asymmetric νₐₛ(C–D) partner is expected near 2160 cm⁻¹ and is not resolved, being buried under κ²-DCOO*.

bands.description: CD₃ asymmetric stretch of deuterated methoxy, the partner of νₛ(CD₃) roughly 110 cm⁻¹ below it. It is the harder of the two to use, because it falls in the middle of the deuterated formate window: wherever a catalyst carries both species, the stronger DCOO* bands bury it and only the symmetric component can be integrated. It becomes visible where formate is scarce, as on an oxide that converts formate onward to methoxy. Adsorbed CO on a reduced metal absorbs in the same region.

references.note: D₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S14; Table S2): the deuterated methoxy made by the surface Ga-D. Table S2 writes only ν(CD) of CD₃O and does not say which CH₃ mode it replaces. It is recorded as the asymmetric one because 2940/2194 = 1.34 matches the νₐₛ(CH₃) the same table reports, while the νₛ(CH₃) at 2834 cm⁻¹ would put its partner near 2080 cm⁻¹; that reading is the atlas's, not the paper's. A second feature marked C-D at 2067 cm⁻¹ in the figure is absent from Table S2 and left unassigned.

bands.description: Methanol O-H stretch (MeOH*/MeOH(g)) — broad and hydrogen-bonding-sensitive like most O-H stretches, so its exact shape depends heavily on the local hydrogen-bonding environment. Often obscured by adsorbed water and surface hydroxyl groups absorbing in the same broad region.

references.note: Table I, CH₃OH vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: ν(OH) Q 3687 cm⁻¹ (vs); R 3713, P 3673; collapses to ~3337 cm⁻¹, very strong and broad, in the liquid due to H-bonding. The CH₃OD counterpart from the same paper's Table II is filed separately — see ν(OD) CH₃OD.

Table 3, ν₁(A′) νOH of CH₃OH isolated in solid neon at 6 K, 0.3 cm⁻¹ resolution. Argon puts it at 3666.7 cm⁻¹: the two hosts differ by 23 cm⁻¹, the largest matrix effect of any methanol fundamental, and they straddle the gas-phase value of 3681.5 cm⁻¹ by +8.6 and −14.8 cm⁻¹. Matrix isolation quenches rotation, so this is a single sharp line rather than the rovibrational envelope the gas-phase band has.

bands.description: O-D stretch of O-deuterated methanol, the hydroxyl counterpart of ν(OH) MeOH nearly 1000 cm⁻¹ lower. Drawn as the full R to P envelope, since all three branches sit inside 40 cm⁻¹. The point of moving the band here is escape: methanol's O-H stretch is the one most easily lost under support hydroxyls and adsorbed water. The escape is only partial, because the new position collides with the C-H stretching region instead.

references.note: Table II, CH₃OD vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: ν(OD) Q 2720 cm⁻¹, R 2745, P 2705. Against Table I's ν(OH) Q at 3687 cm⁻¹ this is Δν(OH→OD) = −967 cm⁻¹, close to the harmonic √2 expectation for an X-H bond and the basis for the assignment.

Table 3, ν₁(A′) νOD of CH₃OD in solid neon at 6 K; 2704.8 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 2717.6 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. Deuterating the hydroxyl leaves the methyl bands almost where they were, which is what makes it the clean way to separate O-H from C-H features.

Table 3, ν₁(A′) νOD of the fully deuterated CD₃OD in solid neon at 6 K; 2705.3 cm⁻¹ in argon. It sits 1.3 cm⁻¹ from the same mode in CH₃OD, which is the point: the O-D stretch does not care whether the methyl group is deuterated, so both are recorded on this one band.

Table IV, CD₃OD vapour: Q branch of the O-D stretch at 2724 cm⁻¹, R 2746 and P 2708 cm⁻¹. Within 4 cm⁻¹ of the same mode in CH₃OD (Table II, 2720 cm⁻¹), which is the vapour-phase version of the point that the O-D stretch does not care whether the methyl group is deuterated.

bands.description: The higher of the two symmetric methyl stretches of methanol, measured on the fully deuterated molecule. Deuteration divides the C-H stretching wavenumbers by roughly 1.33 and moves the whole methyl region from 3000 to 2100 cm⁻¹, where nothing else in a methanol spectrum absorbs. The mode also changes character: on CD₃OD the paper labels it a CD₂ rather than a CD₃ motion, since the in-plane deuteron stops participating.

references.note: Table 3, νₛ(CD₂) of CD₃OD isolated in solid neon at 6 K; 2255.0 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 2250 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. Full deuteration is what lifts the resonances of the light molecule, so this spectrum has fewer bands than CH₃OH rather than the same number moved.

bands.description: The antisymmetric methyl stretch of fully deuterated methanol. In the light molecule this mode is spread across three resonance-mixed bands and cannot be assigned uniquely; deuteration lifts the resonance, leaving one dominant band and a much weaker second one. That simplification is the reason the deuterated spectrum is what settles the assignment of the ordinary one.

references.note: Table 3, νₐₛ(CD₃) of CD₃OD isolated in solid neon at 6 K; 2218.9 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 2212.6 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. Full deuteration is what lifts the resonances of the light molecule, so this spectrum has fewer bands than CH₃OH rather than the same number moved.

Table IV, CD₃OD vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: the antisymmetric CD₃ stretch as a three-component envelope centred on 2228 cm⁻¹, with Barker and Bosschieter's higher-resolution 2227 cm⁻¹ quoted alongside. Falk's own accuracy above 2000 cm⁻¹ is ±4 cm⁻¹. The matrix values are 15 to 20 cm⁻¹ lower, which is the host effect rather than a disagreement.

bands.description: The lower symmetric methyl stretch of fully deuterated methanol, and the strongest band of the deuterated methyl region. Its counterpart in the light molecule is itself half a resonance with the methyl scissor overtone; here the overtone has moved away and the band stands alone.

references.note: Table 3, νₛ(CD₃) of CD₃OD isolated in solid neon at 6 K; 2078.0 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 2074.5 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. Full deuteration is what lifts the resonances of the light molecule, so this spectrum has fewer bands than CH₃OH rather than the same number moved.

Table IV, CD₃OD vapour: Q branch of the symmetric CD₃ stretch at 2080 cm⁻¹, with R at 2100 and P at 2063 cm⁻¹, and 2081 cm⁻¹ from the higher-resolution work the paper prefers. The strongest band of the deuterated methyl region, as in the matrix.

bands.description: Methyl scissor of fully deuterated methanol. The deformation region drops from 1480 to 1450 cm⁻¹ down to 1130 to 1060, where it lands on the C-O stretches instead: deuteration clears the C-H region at the cost of crowding the fingerprint one.

references.note: Table 3, δ(CD₃) of CD₃OD isolated in solid neon at 6 K; 1127.9 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 1133.5 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. Full deuteration is what lifts the resonances of the light molecule, so this spectrum has fewer bands than CH₃OH rather than the same number moved.

Table IV, CD₃OD vapour: Q branch at 1135 cm⁻¹ of an approximately parallel band, R 1155 and P 1117 cm⁻¹, assigned to the symmetric CD₃ bending mode. The paper reads the parallel envelope as the evidence for the assignment, and the polarised Raman band of liquid CD₃OH at 1127 cm⁻¹ as its confirmation.

bands.description: Methyl umbrella deformation of fully deuterated methanol, within a few wavenumbers of the rocking mode and of the C-O scaffold stretch. Three unrelated modes inside 10 cm⁻¹ is what makes the deuterated fingerprint region harder to read than the light one, even though the stretching region becomes easier.

references.note: Table 3, δₛ(CD₃) of CD₃OD isolated in solid neon at 6 K; 1068.2 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 1078 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. Full deuteration is what lifts the resonances of the light molecule, so this spectrum has fewer bands than CH₃OH rather than the same number moved.

bands.description: Rocking deformation of the two out-of-plane deuterons of fully deuterated methanol. It sits below the umbrella mode here, the reverse of the order in the light molecule, which is one of the reasons a notation carried over from CH₃OH mislabels the deuterated spectrum.

references.note: Table 3, ρ(CD₂) of CD₃OD isolated in solid neon at 6 K; 1064.1 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 1069.3 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. Full deuteration is what lifts the resonances of the light molecule, so this spectrum has fewer bands than CH₃OH rather than the same number moved.

bands.description: The mixed C-O stretch of fully deuterated methanol, the one that carries bending character as well. It barely moves on deuteration, which is the evidence that it is the C-O bond rather than the hydrogens that dominates it.

references.note: Table 3, ν(CO) of CD₃OD isolated in solid neon at 6 K; 1031.5 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 1027.8 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. Full deuteration is what lifts the resonances of the light molecule, so this spectrum has fewer bands than CH₃OH rather than the same number moved.

bands.description: The C-O stretch of fully deuterated methanol, some 50 cm⁻¹ below the light molecule. The shift is real but modest, since the mode is only 41% C-O stretch and the rest is bending that the deuterons do slow down.

references.note: Table 3, ν(CO) of CD₃OD isolated in solid neon at 6 K; 983.0 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 980.0 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. Full deuteration is what lifts the resonances of the light molecule, so this spectrum has fewer bands than CH₃OH rather than the same number moved.

Table IV, CD₃OD vapour: Q branch of the C-O stretch at 983 cm⁻¹, R 1001 and P 962 cm⁻¹. The C-O stretch falls from 1034 cm⁻¹ in CH₃OH to 983 cm⁻¹ here, and the paper uses that shift together with the methyl bending shift to argue that the symmetric CH₃ bend and the C-O stretch interact.

bands.description: Methyl twisting deformation of fully deuterated methanol. In the light molecule this is the band with the largest matrix shift of any fundamental; deuterated, it moves to a quieter part of the spectrum where the host matters less.

references.note: Table 3, δₐₛ(CD₃) of CD₃OD isolated in solid neon at 6 K; 895.0 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 892 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. Full deuteration is what lifts the resonances of the light molecule, so this spectrum has fewer bands than CH₃OH rather than the same number moved.

bands.description: In-plane C-O-D bend of deuterated methanol, roughly 550 cm⁻¹ below the C-O-H bend it comes from, because this is the mode that swings the hydroxyl hydrogen. That very large shift is what makes it a clean test of whether a band in the fingerprint region involves the hydroxyl at all.

references.note: Table 3, δ(COD) of CD₃OD isolated in solid neon at 6 K; 775.9 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 774.8 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. Full deuteration is what lifts the resonances of the light molecule, so this spectrum has fewer bands than CH₃OH rather than the same number moved.
Table IV, CD₃OD vapour: Q branch at 776 cm⁻¹, R 797 and P 753 cm⁻¹, assigned jointly to CD₃ rocking and the in-plane O-D bend, which the paper says are mixed in this molecule rather than separable.

bands.description: R-branch rotational satellite of gas-phase methanol ν(OH); ~26 cm⁻¹ above the Q branch at 3687 cm⁻¹. Only present in gas-phase spectra.

references.note: Table I, CH₃OH vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: ν(OH) R branch at 3713 cm⁻¹.

bands.description: P-branch rotational satellite of gas-phase methanol ν(OH); ~14 cm⁻¹ below the Q branch at 3687 cm⁻¹. Only present in gas-phase spectra.

references.note: Table I, CH₃OH vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: ν(OH) P branch at 3673 cm⁻¹.

bands.description: One of methanol's two symmetric-species CH₃ stretches (see the vibration-modes page for why this isn't "the asymmetric one") — sits close enough to the O-H stretch's low-wavenumber tail that the two can blur together in a broad surface spectrum.

references.note: Table 3, ν₂(A′) νsCH₃ of CH₃OH in solid neon at 6 K; 3006.4 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 2999.0 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. This is the higher of methanol's two symmetric methyl stretches, 78% of the motion on the in-plane hydrogen, which is why it is not the asymmetric one despite sitting highest.

Fig. 4a/4c (2985 cm⁻¹; the main text quotes 2981 cm⁻¹ for the same feature) and Fig. 5b (2994 cm⁻¹) — operando DRIFTS, 230 °C, 10–20 bar, H₂/CO₂ = 3, Cu–M/SiO₂ from SOMC. In the SI, Fig. S17 gives 2996 cm⁻¹ (Cu–In/SiO₂) and Fig. S20 2994 cm⁻¹ (Cu–Ga/SiO₂, labelled explicitly as adsorbed methanol inside a component non-separable from κ²-HCOO*(Ga³⁺) and CH₃O*(Ga³⁺)); Table S1 quotes 2996 cm⁻¹. Assigned there as νₐₛ(C–H) of molecularly adsorbed CH₃OH*, filed under this band on position rather than on that label, since gas-phase methanol's own ν₂/ν₉ assignment in this region is resonance-mixed (see νₐₛ(CH₃) CH₃OH* below). Builds up only after ~90 min, and its delay relative to the mass-spectrometer CH₃OH signal is read as product methanol being re-adsorbed on silica rather than desorbing straight out.

bands.description: The antisymmetric stretch of methanol’s two out-of-plane C-H bonds, a CH₂ rather than a CH₃ motion: the in-plane hydrogen barely moves. Typically 10 to 20 cm⁻¹ above methoxy in the same region, which is the cleanest way to tell molecularly adsorbed methanol from methoxy. In the isolated molecule it is not one band: it is spread across three, mixed with combinations of the methyl deformations, and no single band is dominated by the fundamental. That structure washes out on a working catalyst, but it is why the position quoted for this mode varies by tens of cm⁻¹ between sources.

references.note: Removed by evacuation at 200 °C, leaving methoxy on the surface.

Table I, CH₃OH vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: νas(CH₃) at 2973 cm⁻¹ (vs); Falk treats a′ and a″ asymmetric stretches as one unresolved envelope — later work (Serrallach 1974, Dinu 2024) identifies this as a 3-component Fermi-resonance multiplet rather than a single fundamental.

Table 3 and Fig. 7a: in solid neon at 6 K this mode is not one band but three, at 2966.9, 2928.2 and 2912.0 cm⁻¹ (2961.8, 2930.0 and 2914.2 in argon). The VCI analysis finds no state dominated by the ν₉ fundamental: 2966.9 cm⁻¹ is 59.9% the ν₄+ν₁₀ combination against 28.3% ν₉, and 2912.0 cm⁻¹ is best labelled ν₅+ν₁₀. Deuterating the methyl group collapses the pattern, which is how the resonance is demonstrated. Assigning a single band here to an asymmetric methyl stretch is the misassignment this paper exists to correct.

bands.description: Adsorbed methanol CH₃ symmetric stretch, 10 to 20 cm⁻¹ above methoxy νₛ(CH₃), which is what separates molecular methanol from the methoxy it converts into; the two appear as a shoulder pair and mild evacuation removes the methanol first. It also falls under the gas-phase Q branch of the same mode, so surface and gas contributions sit on top of each other, and the flanking R and P satellites are what tell them apart.

references.note: Methanol dosed on TiO₂; removed by evacuation at 200 °C together with the νₐₛ(CH₃) partner, leaving methoxy on the surface.

bands.description: Q-branch head of gas-phase methanol νₛ(CH₃), the central and strongest of the three branches, with R about 24 cm⁻¹ above and P about 19 cm⁻¹ below. It falls on the adsorbed-methanol and methoxy νₛ(CH₃) region, so gas and surface overlap over a working catalyst; the flanking satellites identify the gas part, since an adsorbed species has no rotational structure.

references.note: Table I, CH₃OH vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: ν₃ νs(CH₃) Q 2845 cm⁻¹ (s); R 2869, P 2826.

Table 3, ν₃(A′) νsCH₃ of CH₃OH in solid neon at 6 K; 2848.0 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 2844.2 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. The VCI wave function is 51% this fundamental and 26% the first overtone of the methyl scissor, so even the cleanest-looking band in this region is a resonance rather than a pure fundamental.

bands.description: R-branch rotational satellite of gas-phase methanol νs(CH₃); ~24 cm⁻¹ above the Q branch at 2845 cm⁻¹. Only present in gas-phase spectra.

references.note: Table I, CH₃OH vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: νs(CH₃) R branch at 2869 cm⁻¹.

bands.description: P-branch rotational satellite of gas-phase methanol νs(CH₃); ~19 cm⁻¹ below the Q branch at 2845 cm⁻¹. Only present in gas-phase spectra.

references.note: Table I, CH₃OH vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: νs(CH₃) P branch at 2826 cm⁻¹.

bands.description: Methanol CH₃ scissor deformation (MeOH*/MeOH(g)) — frequency-coincident with the rocking mode just below it; the two are rarely resolved separately in catalytic DRIFTS.

references.note: Table I, CH₃OH vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: δas(CH₃) a′ at 1477 cm⁻¹ (m).
Table 3, ν₄(A′) δCH₃ scissor of CH₃OH in solid neon at 6 K; 1473.5 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 1477.2 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase.

bands.description: First overtone of the methanol CH₃ scissor deformation — weak, and falls right in the middle of the C-H stretching region, where it resonance-mixes with the genuine stretch fundamentals (see νₐₛ(CH₂) above).

references.note: Fig. 6d, the observed neon-matrix band at 2954.0 cm⁻¹ (2955.9 in argon, Fig. 6a), assigned to 2ν₄ by the VCI calculation, which puts it at 2955 cm⁻¹. It is the one overtone in this region the calculation can assign uniquely for CH₃OH: 2ν₁₀ and 2ν₅ are spread across three states near 2928, 2922 and 2847 cm⁻¹ and cannot be pinned to single bands.

bands.description: Methanol CH₂ rocking deformation (MeOH*/MeOH(g)) — only the two out-of-plane H's participate (see the vibration-modes page); sits just below the scissor mode above, close enough that the two rarely resolve separately in catalytic DRIFTS.

references.note: Table 3, ν₁₀(A″) δasCH₂ rocking of CH₃OH in solid neon at 6 K; 1466.3 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 1465 ± 3 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. Matrix isolation separates it from the scissor 8 cm⁻¹ above, which the older gas-phase compilation reported at the same position as the scissor.

Not recorded as a position: Falk assigns the third methyl deformation to a band at 1415 cm⁻¹ in the CH₃OH vapour and the two methyl rocking modes to 1233 and 1116 cm⁻¹, an assignment his own abstract flags as differing from earlier work and which later gas-phase and matrix studies overturned. The mode this band carries is now placed near 1465 cm⁻¹, between the scissor and the umbrella. The 1961 numbers are kept here as the historical reading rather than as a competing measurement.

bands.description: Methanol CH₃ umbrella deformation (MeOH*/MeOH(g)) — sits just below the scissor/rock pair above; all three of these δCH₃-region fundamentals cluster within ~25 cm⁻¹ of each other.

references.note: Table I, CH₃OH vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: δs(CH₃) a′ at 1455 cm⁻¹ (m).

Table 3, ν₅(A′) δCH₃ umbrella of CH₃OH in solid neon at 6 K; 1451.8 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 1454.5 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. Its first overtone is one of the states the 2960 to 2900 cm⁻¹ resonance pattern is built from.

bands.description: Methanol C-O-H in-plane bend (MeOH*/MeOH(g)) — weak, and sits at the low-wavenumber edge of the formate νₛ(OCO) region, so it's easy to miss against a stronger neighboring band.

references.note: Table I, CH₃OH vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: δip(OH) at 1346 cm⁻¹ (s). Falk value (1346) agrees with Shimanouchi (1345) but is ~14 cm⁻¹ above Serrallach 1974 (1332); discrepancy attributed by Falk to coupling between δ(OH) a′ and ρ(CH₃) a′ motions.

Table 3, ν₆(A′) δipOH of CH₃OH in solid neon at 6 K; 1329.6 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 1332.0 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. The 1345 cm⁻¹ of the older compilation is 13 cm⁻¹ off and is the value most often carried forward in the literature.

bands.description: Methanol CH₃ twisting deformation (MeOH*/MeOH(g)) — only the two out-of-plane H's participate, one swinging toward the C-O axis and the other away (see the vibration-modes page).

references.note: Table 3, ν₁₁(A″) δasCH₃ twisting of CH₃OH in solid neon at 6 K; 1162.8 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 1145 ± 4 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. The 11 to 18 cm⁻¹ blue shift is the largest matrix effect of any methanol fundamental apart from the O-H stretch, so this position is host-dependent and should not be read as a free-molecule value.

bands.description: Methanol's second, more delocalized C-O-region fundamental (MeOH*/MeOH(g)) — mixes C-O stretching with C-O-H/O-C-H angle bending rather than being a clean bond stretch like the band below; distinguishing the two in practice relies on the C-H stretching region markers, not position alone.

references.note: Table 3, ν₇(A′) νCO scaffold of CH₃OH in solid neon at 6 K; 1076.3 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 1074.5 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase. Only 72% of this mode is the C-O stretch; the rest is HOC and OCH bending, which is why methanol has two bands in this region rather than one.

bands.description: Methanol C-O stretch (MeOH*/MeOH(g)). Falls in the 1000–1200 cm⁻¹ window shared with monodentate and bidentate methoxy ν(C-O); CH₃OH(a) and CH₃O(a) routinely coexist after low-temperature alcohol dosing and contribute jointly to this region. Disambiguate via the CH₃ stretching region: adsorbed methanol shows νₐₛ/νₛ blue-shifted by ~10–20 cm⁻¹ relative to methoxy.

references.note: Fig. 1b (ME-DRIFTS-PSD, Cu-GaZrOₓ, 20 bar, 260 °C): CH₃OH(g) is followed as the product of the modulation experiment and appears in the spectra below 1100 cm⁻¹, but the paper marks it by label rather than by wavenumber, so no position is recorded here. Its phase delay behind CH₃O* is the paper's evidence that methoxy is hydrolysed to methanol rather than hydrogenated.

Table I, CH₃OH vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: ν(CO) P/Q/R branches at 1012/1034/1060 cm⁻¹ (vs). Q branch at 1034 is the fundamental; R at 1060 cm⁻¹ coincides with the CO scaffold mode (~1074 cm⁻¹) and may cause apparent broadening on the high-frequency side.

Table 3, ν₈(A′) νCO of CH₃OH in solid neon at 6 K; 1033.9 cm⁻¹ in argon, against 1033.5 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase, the smallest matrix shift of any methanol fundamental. Despite the label it is only 41% C-O stretch, with 29% HOC and 28% OCH bending mixed in.

bands.description: First overtone of the methanol C-O stretch, weak but sitting squarely in the window where CO on a reduced metal absorbs. Gas-phase methanol over a working catalyst therefore puts a band near 2056 cm⁻¹ that has nothing to do with adsorbed CO, with its R and P branches about 20 cm⁻¹ either side. Rotational structure is the discriminator: an adsorbed carbonyl has none. It moves with the C-O fundamental on deuteration, to about 1960 cm⁻¹ in the fully deuterated molecule.

references.note: Table I, CH₃OH vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: Q branch at 2056 cm⁻¹, R 2078 and P 2035 cm⁻¹, assigned to 2×1034 and so to the overtone of the C-O stretch. The same overtone appears in all four methanols the paper measured: 2062 cm⁻¹ in CH₃OD, 1966 in CD₃OH and 1959 cm⁻¹ in CD₃OD.

bands.description: R-branch rotational satellite of gas-phase methanol ν(CO); ~26 cm⁻¹ above the Q branch at 1034 cm⁻¹. Overlaps with the CO scaffold mode (νCO* fundamental at 1074 cm⁻¹) — the two cannot be distinguished by position alone in DRIFTS.

references.note: Table I, CH₃OH vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: ν(CO) R branch at 1060 cm⁻¹ (vs).

bands.description: P-branch rotational satellite of gas-phase methanol ν(CO); ~22 cm⁻¹ below the Q branch at 1034 cm⁻¹. Only present in gas-phase spectra.

references.note: Table I, CH₃OH vapour in a 10-cm cell at 80 mmHg and room temperature: ν(CO) P branch at 1012 cm⁻¹.

bands.description: Surface hydroxyl stretch on an oxide: the O-H left behind wherever water or H₂ dissociates on it. The window is wide because the position tracks the coordination of the cation carrying the group and how strongly it is hydrogen-bonded. Discrete sharp components above roughly 3600 cm⁻¹ come from terminal hydroxyls on distinct cation environments, and hydrogen bonding drags them down and merges them into a broad envelope. Counting the sharp components is how the kinds of cation site a surface exposes get counted. The region is normally read as a difference spectrum, since adsorbates consume hydroxyls and push the band negative.

references.note: Fig. 1 (precipitated Ga₂O₃, 0.1 MPa H₂ at 450 °C): the higher of two hydroxyls resolved on one surface, assigned to the OH on a tetrahedrally coordinated gallium and formed together with the Ga-H at 2011 cm⁻¹. The split from the other hydroxyl follows the two gallium coordinations, not hydrogen bonding. Both O-H bands are about five times weaker than the hydride bands they accompany, the opposite of the usual intensity order, which the authors read as evidence that hydride rather than hydroxyl is what accumulates here.

Fig. 1 (precipitated Ga₂O₃, 0.1 MPa H₂ at 450 °C): the lower of the two hydroxyls, on an octahedrally coordinated gallium, formed together with the Ga-H at 1988 cm⁻¹. Two claims rather than one array, because the paper assigns each position to its own gallium site.

Fig. S4 (as-prepared precipitated Ga₂O₃ referenced to KBr; the geometry is not stated): a broad hydroxyl envelope centred near 3450 cm⁻¹, with an OH bend marked near 1640 cm⁻¹. This is the oxide before any H₂ treatment, and the paper uses it to argue that the surface already carries a substantial hydroxyl coverage, so the sharp 3685 and 3532 cm⁻¹ pair grown under H₂ at 450 °C is a small addition to an already hydroxylated surface. Both numbers are approximate in the figure's own labels.

Fig. 2 (hydroxylated nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃, 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K): both bands appear as negative peaks, since CO₂ consumes these hydroxyls to make bicarbonate. They are assigned to OH bonded to two and to three iron atoms respectively, with singly coordinated hydroxyls expected near 3700 cm⁻¹ and more highly coordinated ones lower. A broad band near 3300 cm⁻¹ is the hydrogen-bonded population.

Fig. 7 region and the accompanying text (IRRAS, UHV, room temperature): O-H stretching modes found around 3640 cm⁻¹ on both magnetite facets. The polarization gives the tilt: roughly 45° from the surface normal for surface hydroxyls and about 75° for the O-H of molecularly adsorbed formic acid. These hydroxyls are where the hydrogen released by the dissociating acid ends up. The paper cautions that O-H bands on magnetite are intrinsically very weak, so the calculated positions could not be checked against experiment.

Fig. 1 (commercial silica, 312 m²/g, annealed in flowing Ar at 350 °C for 5 min, then cooled to 50 °C in 50 °C steps, background the SiC-filled cell): free silanols. Beside them a larger band from 3800 to 3000 cm⁻¹ of hydrogen-bonded silanols, which grows slightly on cooling, most likely as traces of water readsorb.

Fig. 2 (the same silica at 50, 150 and 250 °C in Ar, referenced to its own spectrum at 350 °C): new free silanols at 3743 cm⁻¹ and hydrogen-bonded hydroxyls around 3445 cm⁻¹, both clearer the lower the temperature, as the surface partly rehydrates. The same difference spectra grow spurious bands in the carbonyl region (see lattice overtones SiO₂).

bands.description: A surface hydroxyl measured under D₂ or D₂O. The O-D stretch sits at about 1/1.36 of the O-H position, moving the hydroxyl region from 3400 to 3750 cm⁻¹ down into 2500 to 2750 cm⁻¹, where little else on an oxide absorbs. The pattern of components survives the shift, so it is the cleanest way to prove a band is a hydroxyl and to count how many kinds a surface carries. It overlaps the C-D stretches of deuterated adsorbates.

references.note: Figs. 1 and S3 (precipitated Ga₂O₃, 0.1 MPa D₂ at 450 °C): the deuterated counterpart of the 3685 and 3532 cm⁻¹ hydroxyl pair, formed alongside the Ga-D bands. Both components are recorded on this one band because the paper reports them together and does not pair each with its own hydroxyl, though the ratios (1.37 and 1.36) follow the same order.

bands.description: Gas-phase water symmetric O-H stretch (ν₁, A₁): both O-H bonds lengthening and shortening together, in phase. The number is the band origin, not the feature you see. Water is a light asymmetric top with widely spaced rotational levels, so each fundamental is a rovibrational envelope hundreds of cm⁻¹ across, built from sharp individual lines: the sharpness belongs to the lines, the band is wide. It overlaps ν₃ throughout, and the two are separable only by line position. Adsorbed or condensed water loses the rotation and gives one broad merged feature instead (see oh_surface).

references.note: ν₁, the symmetric stretch. Herzberg's book tabulates the gas-phase fundamentals of H₂O; this is the band origin, not a measured peak width or a value from one spectrum. Recorded without a technique because the book compiles results from many sources rather than reporting its own. Caveat on the source itself: the PDF filed against this citekey is Bryce Crawford's one-page review of the book (J. Phys. Chem. 50, 288, 1946), not the book, so the number here is the standard tabulated value and the book itself was not opened.

bands.description: Gas-phase water H-O-H angle bend (ν₂, A₁), the only bend a three-atom molecule has and the strongest of the three fundamentals. The recorded number is the band origin; the observed envelope runs roughly 1300 to 2100 cm⁻¹ as a comb of sharp rotational lines, which is why water vapour in the beam is the standard nuisance across the carbonate, formate and carbonyl region. Purging or subtracting a matched vapour spectrum is the usual remedy, and residual lines here are an artefact rather than a surface species.

references.note: ν₂, the bend, and the strongest of the three. Herzberg's book tabulates the gas-phase fundamentals of H₂O; this is the band origin, not a measured peak width or a value from one spectrum. Recorded without a technique because the book compiles results from many sources rather than reporting its own. Caveat on the source itself: the PDF filed against this citekey is Bryce Crawford's one-page review of the book (J. Phys. Chem. 50, 288, 1946), not the book, so the number here is the standard tabulated value and the book itself was not opened.

bands.description: Gas-phase water asymmetric O-H stretch (ν₃, B₂): one O-H bond lengthening while the other shortens, out of phase. The highest of the three fundamentals, about 100 cm⁻¹ above the symmetric stretch, and the two envelopes overlap so completely that only the line positions separate them. Like the other two it is a wide rovibrational envelope of sharp lines rather than one narrow band, and it collapses into the broad hydroxyl feature once the molecule is adsorbed or condensed.

references.note: ν₃, the asymmetric stretch and the highest of the three fundamentals. Herzberg's book tabulates the gas-phase fundamentals of H₂O; this is the band origin, not a measured peak width or a value from one spectrum. Recorded without a technique because the book compiles results from many sources rather than reporting its own. Caveat on the source itself: the PDF filed against this citekey is Bryce Crawford's one-page review of the book (J. Phys. Chem. 50, 288, 1946), not the book, so the number here is the standard tabulated value and the book itself was not opened.

bands.description: Terminal hydride on a gallium centre: H₂ dissociated on the oxide itself rather than on a metal particle. Heterolytic splitting across a Ga-O pair puts a hydride on Ga and a proton on lattice oxygen, so Ga-H and fresh O-H bands appear together; the two gallium coordinations split it by about 25 cm⁻¹. On a reduced surface H₂ can split homolytically instead, into two hydrides and no new O-H, so the hydroxyl is not a count of the hydride. It sits in the CO stretching window, which is the standing confusion, and deuteration to near 1435 cm⁻¹ settles it. Metal-H absorbs far more weakly than O-H, so intensity is a poor guide to coverage.

references.note: Fig. 4b to 4d (ME-DRIFTS, Cu-free GaZrOₓ, 1 bar and 20 bar, 260 °C): ν(Ga-H) at 1976 cm⁻¹, strong on the oxide alone (about 0.03 Kubelka-Munk in Fig. 4d). The assignment is confirmed by feeding D₂ in place of H₂: the band is absent under CO₂+D₂ (Fig. 4c). No Ga-D counterpart is reported anywhere in the paper or its SI, so the evidence is the disappearance, not a measured shift. The band stays largely static through the modulation, which the authors read as a slow step: Ga-H reduces (bi)carbonates to HCOO* and helps hydrogenate HCOO* to CH₃O*.

Fig. 1b (ME-DRIFTS-PSD, Cu-GaZrOₓ, 20 bar, 260 °C): the same hydride on the Cu-containing sample, marked at 1980 cm⁻¹, four wavenumbers above the value quoted for the Cu-free oxide. It is far weaker here, near 0.001 against 0.03 Kubelka-Munk on GaZrOₓ (Fig. 4d), which is the paper's argument that Ga-H accumulates on the oxide and is consumed quickly once Cu is present.

Fig. 1 (in-situ DRIFTS, precipitated Ga₂O₃, 0.1 MPa H₂ at 450 °C, referenced to the same sample under Ar): the weaker, higher component of the hydride pair, assigned to H on tetrahedrally coordinated gallium together with the O-H at 3685 cm⁻¹. The pair is split by about 25 cm⁻¹, which the authors attribute to the two Ga coordinations of the bulk oxide rather than to two different kinds of hydride. Their own DFT cuts against this component: it finds the four-fold surface Ga saturated and Ga(t)-H formation impossible, leaving only the unsaturated Ga(o) able to take a hydrogen. The paper does not reconcile the two.

Fig. 1: the dominant component of the hydride pair on precipitated Ga₂O₃ under 0.1 MPa H₂ at 450 °C, assigned to H on octahedrally coordinated gallium with the O-H at 3532 cm⁻¹. Formation needs temperature: the band is weak at room temperature and grows monotonically above 150 °C (Fig. 2a), matching the onset of H₂-D₂ exchange. Ar purging removes it within 30 min at 450 °C and it returns on re-admitting H₂, so the dissociation is reversible (Figs. S5, S6). Coverage tracks the pretreatment, O₂ < Ar < H₂ (Fig. S9). It is inert to CO₂, CO, O₂, N₂ and Ar at 150 °C; at 200 °C both O₂ and CO₂ consume it, giving water and formate, while N₂ and CO leave it untouched even above 450 °C (Fig. 4).

bands.description: The Ga-H stretch measured under D₂. A metal deuteride sits at about 1/1.39 of its hydride position, the square root of the reduced-mass ratio, so the pair moves from near 2000 to near 1435 cm⁻¹ and keeps its splitting. Nothing else in a CO₂ hydrogenation spectrum moves that far on deuteration, which is what makes it diagnostic; it lands among the carbonate and formate bands, which is what makes it easy to miss.

references.note: Figs. 1 and S3 (in-situ DRIFTS, precipitated Ga₂O₃, 0.1 MPa D₂ at 450 °C): the deuteride pair, with the same shoulder-plus-main shape as the hydride pair and in the same intensity order, so 1442 cm⁻¹ pairs with 2011 cm⁻¹ and 1430 cm⁻¹ with 1988 cm⁻¹. The measured ν(Ga-H)/ν(Ga-D) ratio is 1.39 against 1.40 from the reduced masses. The paper does not assign the two deuteride components to the two Ga coordinations itself, so only the generic Ga centre is recorded here. A D₂ temperature-programmed surface reaction after CO₂ adsorption puts the band at 1429 cm⁻¹ (Fig. S14).

bands.description: Terminal hydride on a zinc centre, the zinc counterpart of the gallium hydride: H₂ split heterolytically across a Zn-O pair leaves a hydride on the cation and a proton on lattice oxygen. It absorbs far below a metal carbonyl and lands instead among the C=O stretches of surface formic acid, formate and formyl, which is the standing ambiguity: a band near 1690 cm⁻¹ on a zinc oxide catalyst has been read both ways, and the sources that report it do not separate the two. Deuteration would settle it, moving ν(Zn-D) to roughly 1200 cm⁻¹.

references.note: Table 3 and Fig. 3B, 30 bar. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. A small feature at 1691 cm⁻¹, tabulated as ν(C=O) of more strongly surface-bound formic acid or, with the authors’ own question mark, as ν(Zn-H); they cite 1660, 1707 and 1688/1678 cm⁻¹ from the literature for the hydride and none for the acid. One of four bands (1759, 1691, 1457 and 1398 cm⁻¹) whose intensity rises with the GHSV and with the methanol in the outlet gas, which is why the paper counts it among the true intermediates rather than the spectators. No isotope experiment is offered that would separate the two readings.

bands.description: Not a vibration. An electron trapped in a singly ionized oxygen vacancy of reduced zinc oxide, lifted into the conduction band by the infrared beam itself. It absorbs as one featureless rise about 2000 cm⁻¹ wide running under the whole carbonyl and fingerprint region, so every band drawn on top of it sits on a sloping baseline rather than a flat one. Its maximum reports on the metal-oxide contact: near 1000 cm⁻¹ on zinc oxide alone and near 1500 cm⁻¹ once copper is present. It needs hydrogen to exist, vanishing under nitrogen, and is strongest under methanol synthesis conditions.

references.note: Figs. 5 and 6, 30 bar. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. Operando over 54 h with the outlet gas on a GC. Absent under N₂; it appears at once under pure H₂ with a maximum near 1400 cm⁻¹, and on switching to 3H₂/CO₂ it shifts to about 1500 cm⁻¹ (0.19 eV) and grows. It is strongest under methanol synthesis and falls back under intermittent N₂ or CO₂, but it does not follow the methanol production rate itself. Assigned to photoionization of Vₒ⁺ donor centres into the conduction band of the n-type oxide, and its intensity proposed as an online measure of the Cu-ZnO interaction. The main text puts the maximum near 1000 cm⁻¹ for copper-free ZnO, from a supporting-information figure not read here.

bands.description: Not an adsorbate. Overtones and combinations of the Si-O-Si framework vibrations of silica itself, which absorbs so strongly in its fundamentals that little below about 1600 cm⁻¹ survives in diffuse reflectance. The clearest pair sits near 1870 and 1985 cm⁻¹, in the window of bridged and linear metal carbonyls; silicas and zeolites carry more of the series between 1400 and 2800 cm⁻¹. Their shape and position move with temperature and with rehydration, so a difference spectrum referenced to a background at another temperature grows peaks and valleys here that belong to neither spectrum and read convincingly as adsorbed CO. A background taken on the same sample at the same temperature and humidity removes them.

references.note: Fig. 1 (commercial silica, 312 m²/g, annealed in Ar at 350 °C, cooled to 50 °C in 50 °C steps, background the SiC-filled cell): combination and overtone bands of the silica backbone, whose intensity and position change on cooling and rehydration. Referenced to the 350 °C spectrum instead (Fig. 2), that change shows up as new bands at 2036 and 1902 cm⁻¹ and valleys at 1947 and 1823 cm⁻¹, none at the positions of the sample spectrum. The paper warns these could be taken for CO on a silica-supported metal, and the valleys for a vanishing species. The assignment is inherited from the silica literature it cites.
